Level 2 — gating, read-outs and the PA-protection poll
TDD gating. Channel power uses gate view ON, a 1 ms gate (one DL slot) and 10 averages. The gate delay comes from a map keyed by the TDD configuration: config 2 → 18.46 ms (calibrated on one vendor's RU), config 3 → 21 ms, anything else → 15.3 ms. A wrong delay puts the gate on UL or guard symbols, so power reads low and ACLR/EVM look terrible. The n78 SmokeTest group uses ext_trig_delay = 0.00998675 s (about 9.99 ms, close to one 10 ms frame minus a small offset, the same idea as the B41 9.9765 ms in B41T).
sa_set_gate_view_state('ON')
sa_set_trigger_gate_length(0.001)                           <- :SENSe:PVTime:GATE:LENGth
sa_set_trigger_gate_delay(tdd_gate_delay_map.get(cfg, '15.3 ms'))  <- :GATE:DELay
ON/OFF:  :CONF:PVT  ->  :INIT:PVT   with   :TRIG:PVT:SOUR EXT2
TAE:     :DISPlay:EVM:VIEW MIMO ; :SENSe:RADio:MIMO:STATe 1 ; :FETCH:EVM000030?
TAE read-out. The MIMO summary table is one comma-separated list. The TAE values sit at indices [6, 28, 50, 72, 94]. The harness takes abs(), drops values ≥1e30 (the analyzer's "invalid" marker) and reports the max. If nothing is valid it returns −999, which fails the test. The validator gives three states: ≤65 ns Pass, 65–90 ns Marginal, above 90 ns Fail. The usual −999 fixes: MIMO state not enabled, signal below about −30 dBm at the analyzer, or a misaligned TDD trigger. Then preset, wait ~3 s and read again.

SEM reference level. This is the analyzer reference level (headroom above the average power), not a limit. OFDM test models peak several dB above average. Too low a reference level clips the analyzer's front end/ADC, and the clipping splatter looks like DUT emissions. Too high a level buries the mask in analyzer noise. The harness uses +7 dB for the wideband n78 carriers and +6 dB for the 10 MHz n101 carrier.

PA protection (test_Tx_Pa_Protection, GRDEV-6801). The method: read the FHGW DAC current at nominal (carrier inactive) with rfdc-app --debug, activate the carrier, then poll for 25 s. That window covers the ~10 s gain_delay_time PA-warm-up plateau plus ~15 s of carrier-ready latency. The harness latches the deepest dip per DAC block and passes if the reduction is 3.0 ± 0.2 dB. Polling replaced a single timed read that failed whenever the carrier came up late. A result near 0 dB is logged with both possible causes: the PA really is off, or the carrier took longer than the window to reach READY. In 5G it runs once at the top of test_main_procedure, before the per-group loop, and a FAIL does not abort the suite. DAC_MAP maps (fhgw_band, band) to tiles/blocks, and a missing row raises a clear RuntimeError.

SmokeTest path (GRDEV-6620). A group whose Tests list contains test_PreChecks starts TX (M-plane update → TM → PHY), runs the n78 pre-checks (FC12), writes the PreChecks sheet, calls pytest.fail() if the overall result is FAIL, and then breaks the group loop. A smoke run never continues into conformance.
Level 3 — corrections and pitfalls
1. ACLR numbers in the internal doc. The doc says "offset A < −30 dBc, offset B < −33 dBc". Those match the UE ACLR requirements (NR 30 dB, UTRA 33 dB). The NR BS requirement in 38.104 §6.6.3 is 45 dB for the first and second adjacent channels, with an absolute alternative, so the less stringent of the two applies. PW KPI tables also gate at about 45 dB (KPI01, ACLREVM01). If a report passes at 31 dB against the doc limit, the conformance claim is wrong.

2. The spurious sweep must go higher than you think. For NR the upper end of the spurious range is 12.75 GHz or the 5th harmonic of the upper DL band edge, whichever is greater. For n78 (3.8 GHz) that is 19 GHz. An EXM-class analyzer tops out near 6 GHz, which is why the doc insists on a PXA/UXA-class analyzer for 6.6.5. Also plan a high-pass or notch filter so the carrier does not overload the analyzer while it looks for −30 dBm harmonics.

3. OFF power is a noise-floor measurement. −85 dBm/MHz sits just above an unpreamped analyzer's floor. Add a 30 dB coupler/attenuator and it may not be measurable at all. The 70/N µs window is short: at 30 kHz SCS, N = 2, so about 35 µs. The trigger must place that window inside the UL period and away from the ramps. Check the analyzer floor with the DUT off before trusting an OFF-power pass.

4. Pattern labels in comments are not the pattern. The gate-delay map comments describe config 2 and 3 with slot strings that do not match the usual LTE UL/DL configuration table. Derive the gate from the actual configured slot pattern and trigger offset, and re-calibrate the delay on each bench and RU vendor. "Calibrated on one vendor's RU" is the honest label.

5. TAE is a relative number. A 20 cm cable-length mismatch is about 1 ns, so cables rarely explain a 100 ns TAE. Look at per-chain digital delay, JESD lane alignment or a mis-set per-antenna delay compensation (FC05). And remember that TAE compares antenna connectors. Measuring through unequal splitter paths adds error of your own.
Interview Q&A
Q: What does the TX ON/OFF power test check on an NR TDD BS, and what are the limits?
A: In UL periods the transmitter OFF power must be below −85 dBm/MHz, averaged over 70/N µs with N = SCS/15. The OFF→ON and ON→OFF transient periods must each be under 10 µs (LTE allows 17 µs). It protects the BS's own and neighbouring receivers in the UL slots.
Q: Your NR ACLR test passes at 32 dB. Is the radio conformant?
A: No. 32 dB passes the UE-style −30 dBc limit printed in the internal doc, but the BS requirement in 38.104 is 45 dB (or the absolute limit, if that is less stringent). Check which limit the KPI file actually applies.
Q: TAE comes back as −999. What happened?
A: −999 is the harness sentinel for "no valid TAE value in the MIMO table". Enable :SENS:RAD:MIMO:STAT 1, make sure every chain is above about −30 dBm at the analyzer, and check the TDD trigger/gate. Then preset and re-read.
Q: Why does the PA-protection test poll for 25 s instead of reading once?
A: The 3 dB reduction appears after carrier activation. It lasts through a ~10 s gain-delay plateau, and the carrier itself can take up to ~15 s to become READY. A single timed read missed the dip whenever activation was slow. Polling and latching the deepest dip removes that race.
Q: How high must a conducted spurious sweep go for n78?
A: To the greater of 12.75 GHz and the 5th harmonic of the upper DL band edge. For n78 (3.8 GHz) that is 19 GHz, so a PXA/UXA-class analyzer is needed, not an EXM.
UPERF01 Conformance Clause 8 — UL performance tests: PUSCH / PUCCH / PRACH under fading (EPA/EVA/ETU, IRC, HARQ) RCT click to expand ▾
In plain English
Clause 7 asks whether the receiver hears a clean signal (sensitivity, blocking). Clause 8 asks whether it still understands a real, messy uplink. The phone is moving, the signal bounces off buildings, and it fades up and down many times a second. So the lab sends standard uplink channels (PUSCH data, PUCCH control, PRACH access) through a fading simulator and adds noise to a set SNR. It then checks that the base station still decodes enough data, detects enough ACKs, or finds enough preambles. Think of a driving test on a wet, bumpy road instead of an empty car park. PRACH (§8.4) already has its own cards (FC10, PRA01, PRACHDM01). This card covers the PUSCH and PUCCH part.
A clause-8 test chain
The TX of the BS can be off. Single carrier only. Tested at the middle frequency, and at the lowest and highest supported channel bandwidths.
Level 1 — channel models and the test list
Propagation models (LTE, TS 36.141 Annex B):
ModelMeaningTaps / max excess delayDoppler used
EPAExtended Pedestrian A: short delay spread7 taps / 410 ns5 Hz
EVAExtended Vehicular A: medium9 taps / 2510 ns5 Hz, 70 Hz
ETUExtended Typical Urban: long delay spread9 taps / 5000 ns70 Hz, 300 Hz
Names read as model + Doppler, e.g. EVA70 = EVA at 70 Hz maximum Doppler. NR (38.141-1 clause 8) uses TDL models the same way: TDLA30-10, TDLB100-400, TDLC300-100 (delay spread in ns, then Doppler in Hz).

LTE clause 8 test list (TS 36.141):
ClauseTestPass metric
8.2.1PUSCH in multipath fading, single antenna portthroughput ≥ the table value (30 % or 70 % of max) at the given SNR, HARQ on
8.2.2UL timing adjustment (a moving UE + a stationary UE at equal power)moving-UE throughput ≥ 70 %
8.2.3HARQ-ACK multiplexed on PUSCHP(ACK detect) ≥ 0.99 and P(false ACK) ≤ 0.01
8.2.5PUSCH with TTI bundling + enhanced HARQ (FDD only, FRC A11)residual BLER < 2 %
8.2.6 / 8.2.6APUSCH Type A (IRC receiver) with synchronous / asynchronous interferencethroughput ≥ 70 %
8.3.1 / 8.3.3PUCCH format 1a ACK missed detection, single user / multi user (3 interferers on the same RBs)P(ACK detect) ≥ 0.99, P(false detect) ≤ 0.01
8.3.2CQI on PUCCH format 2 (4-bit CQI)CQI BLER < 1 %
8.3.4PUCCH 1b with channel selection (only 10/15/20 MHz)as 8.3.1
8.3.5 / 8.3.6PUCCH format 3 ACK missed detection / NACK→ACKas 8.3.1; NACK→ACK ≤ 0.001 (TDD only)
8.4PRACH false alarm and detectionPfa ≤ 0.1 %, Pd ≥ 99 % (see FC10)
Level 2 — how the tests are run
A PUSCH example. 5 MHz, 2 RX antennas, normal CP, EPA5, FRC A3-4. The requirement is 30 % of maximum throughput at −4.1 dB SNR. The procedure: set AWGN to the level in the configuration table, set the FRC, channel model and SNR from the requirement table, run with HARQ retransmissions, and count correctly decoded transport blocks. Throughput = decoded bits / time, compared with the FRC maximum.

PUCCH detection tests alternate "PUCCH sent" and "nothing sent" (noise only, or noise + interferers in the multi-user case). ACK/NACK repetition is disabled. Missed ACKs are counted in the sent periods, and false ACKs in the idle periods. Format 1a carries 1 bit. Format 1b with channel selection carries 4 encoded bits for up to 2 CCs. Format 3 carries up to 10 ACK bits + SR in FDD (20 in TDD), for up to 5 CCs. LTE has formats 1/1a/1b/2/2a/2b/3/4/5 in total.

TTI bundling (8.2.5). Normally a NACK costs an 8 ms round trip before the retransmission. With bundling the UE sends the same PUSCH in 4 consecutive subframes. In the test a new transport block starts every 20 ms, and the residual BLER after HARQ must be < 2 %: A/B, where A = blocks still wrong after retransmissions and B = blocks sent, not counting repeats.

IRC tests (8.2.6/8.2.6A) add dominant interferers on the same RBs, modelling a nearby UE in the next cell: 1 interferer for 2 RX, 2 for 4–8 RX, 16QAM. The asynchronous version offsets the interferers by 0.33 ms, so they do not line up with the wanted subframes. The receiver must use interference rejection combining: it estimates the interference's spatial covariance across the RX branches and steers a null at it. MRC only maximises the wanted SNR and would fail.

Equipment. You need a UE emulator or signal generator with FRC waveforms, a multi-channel fading emulator (one independently faded path per BS RX port, with the defined antenna correlation), and calibrated AWGN. The BS side supplies CRC/ACK/CQI statistics from L1. An internal 2021 overview notes these tests were not part of band qualification. They sit with PHY/receiver validation (compare the third-party PHY matrix, PHYT01), while the lab inventory lists channel emulators among the extra equipment (FWK6).
Level 3 — what makes clause-8 results trustworthy
1. Is HARQ really closed-loop? Throughput requirements assume the UE retransmits after the BS sends NACK. A plain signal generator that plays a fixed waveform cannot react. What you measure then is first-transmission BLER, not HARQ throughput. That is a useful engineering number, but it is not the clause-8 result, so label it. Conformance-grade setups use an emulator that decodes the BS's HARQ feedback (or a defined fixed-retransmission pattern the standard allows).

2. SNR is per receive antenna and the curves are steep. Near the 70 % point a 0.5 dB SNR error can move throughput by 10–20 points. Calibrate the fader's insertion loss per path. Check that the AWGN covers the whole signal bandwidth. Leave crest-factor headroom, because fading adds deep peaks and a clipped generator output adds hidden distortion. Verify the noise level on each RX branch separately. An unbalanced branch looks like a bad receiver.

3. Correlation and timing matter. Fading paths that are more correlated than specified remove diversity gain, and the DUT fails through no fault of its own. The UL timing adjustment test uses a moving propagation condition, where the path delay slides back and forth. It exercises the BS timing-advance loop, so it fails for a slow or wrong TA estimator, not for poor sensitivity.

4. Watch for errors in slides and summaries. One internal slide says the moving UE's throughput "shall be ≤ 70 %". The requirement is ≥ 70 %. Detection probabilities are floors (≥ 0.99). False-alarm and NACK→ACK rates are ceilings. When in doubt, reason about which direction is "good" for the operator.
Interview Q&A
Q: How do clause 7 and clause 8 of TS 36.141 differ?
A: Clause 7 covers RF receiver characteristics with static, clean signals: sensitivity, dynamic range, selectivity, blocking, IMD. Clause 8 covers performance: demodulation of PUSCH/PUCCH/PRACH under multipath fading and noise at a defined SNR, with throughput or detection-probability metrics.
Q: What do EPA5, EVA70 and ETU300 mean?
A: Channel model plus maximum Doppler. EPA is short delay spread (410 ns), EVA medium (2.5 µs), ETU long (5 µs). 5/70/300 Hz is the Doppler, i.e. how fast the fading varies. That relates to UE speed and carrier frequency.
Q: What is the pass criterion for PUCCH format 1a ACK detection?
A: At the specified SNR, the ACK detection probability must be at least 0.99 when ACK is sent, and the false-detection probability at most 0.01 when only noise is present.
Q: Why do the Type-A interference tests require an IRC receiver?
A: A dominant co-channel interferer on the same RBs cannot be removed by MRC, which only maximises the wanted SNR. IRC uses the interference covariance across the RX antennas to null it. With N RX antennas it can suppress up to N−1 strong interferers, hence 1 interferer for 2 RX and 2 for 4 or more RX.
Q: Your PUSCH fading result is 8 points below the requirement. What do you check before blaming the PHY?
A: SNR calibration per RX branch (fader loss, AWGN level and bandwidth), fading correlation settings, generator headroom/clipping, and whether HARQ is really closed-loop. Then check the FRC and the channel-model configuration against the requirement table.
OTA01 OTA Conformance Method — EIS, EIRP/TRP, chamber path loss & SG = EIS_target + PathLoss RCT click to expand ▾
In plain English
An AAU or active antenna has no cable connector to clip the analyzer onto. The radio and the antenna are one box. So the lab tests it the way a phone would see it: over the air, inside a shielded, echo-free room (an anechoic chamber). Because the air, the cables and the probe antenna all lose signal, the lab first measures that loss, the path loss, at every frequency and angle. It then adds it back to every reading. For receive tests, the question becomes "how weak can a signal arriving from this direction be and still be decoded?" That is EIS. For transmit tests, it is "how much power comes out in this direction" (EIRP) and "how much in total over the whole sphere" (TRP). SPEC03 lists the NR OTA clauses. This card explains the method and the arithmetic.
The OTA measurement chain and the two formulas that matter
The path-loss table is indexed by (port/polarisation, frequency, azimuth, elevation). It replaces the per-port cable-loss calibration used for conducted tests.
Level 1 — the vocabulary
TermMeaningUsed for
EIRPeffective isotropic radiated power: the power an ideal isotropic antenna would need to give the same field in that direction (P + antenna gain)radiated transmit power per declared beam/direction (NR 38.104 §9 / 38.141-2 §6.2)
TRPtotal radiated power: EIRP integrated over the whole sphere, /4π, both polarisations summedOTA BS output power, and OTA ACLR / unwanted emissions / spurious (TRP-based)
EISequivalent isotropic sensitivity: the power arriving at an ideal isotropic antenna position, from a given direction, that still gives the reference throughput (≥95 %)OTA sensitivity (over the declared direction range) and OTA REFSENS
Path losseverything between the instrument port and the DUT reference point: cable + free-space loss − probe gaincorrecting every SG/SA level
Far fielddistance where the wave front is flat enough: R > 2D²/λ (D = largest DUT dimension)deciding whether a chamber is big enough
Which spec? NR: BS type 1-C is conducted only (38.141-1). 1-H is hybrid, with conducted tests at the transceiver-array connectors plus some OTA. 1-O (FR1) and 2-O (FR2) are fully OTA (38.141-2). For LTE/multi-RAT active antenna systems the equivalent split is TS 37.105 (requirements) with TS 37.145-1 (conducted) and TS 37.145-2 (OTA). The OTA-only requirements are directional: radiated transmit power (EIRP), OTA sensitivity (EIS), spatial emissions.
Level 2 — the arithmetic, step by step
RX worked example (illustrative numbers from an internal draft plan). B3, middle frequency 1747.5 MHz. The target EIS is taken equal to the conducted REFSENS, −101.5 dBm, for illustration. The chamber boresight path loss is 75 dB (feed cable + horn + free space).
SG_amplitude = EIS_target + PathLoss(f, az, el)
             = -101.5 dBm + 75 dB = -26.5 dBm     (gate window e.g. -28.5 ... -24.5 dBm)

Search down until BLER > 5 %, keep the lowest passing SG level:
EIS_measured = SG_min - PathLoss = -27.0 - 75 = -102.0 dBm   -> 0.5 dB better than target
Pass: BLER ≤ 5 % at every (frequency, az, el) point, with at least boresight (az 0°, el 0°), using the A3-x FRC family (A3-4 to A3-7 by bandwidth). For TDD (B41) the SG must burst in step with the UL subframes: :RAD:LTE:UL:TDD:CONF 3, :SSFR 8, TRIG:SOUR FRAME, BURS:STAT ON. A continuous SG would also put energy into DL periods.

TX worked example. B3, 1842.5 MHz, path loss for that TX port at boresight 42.1 dB. It is entered on the SA as an external-gain correction of :CORR:BTS:GAIN -42.1 (loss = negative gain), so the SA reads the value referred to the DUT. Prated = −15.7 dBm. A reading of −15.3 dBm is 0.4 dB off, which passes a ±1.5 dB gate. A reading of −17.6 dBm is 1.9 dB off and fails. Re-run the SA auto-level after each correction, because every (port, freq, angle) has a different path loss.

Sanity-check the path loss with Friis. Free-space loss = 20·log10(4πR/λ). At 1842.5 MHz (λ = 0.163 m) and R = 3 m that gives about 47.3 dB. Subtract a probe horn gain of about 8 dBi and add a few dB of cable, and you land near the 42 dB above. If a table value is 10 dB away from that estimate, suspect the table before the DUT.

Far field check. A 0.3 m radiating aperture at 1.84 GHz needs R > 2·0.3²/0.163 ≈ 1.1 m, which is easy. A 1.6 m multi-band AAU at 700 MHz (λ = 0.43 m) needs about 12 m. That is why large arrays are measured in compact antenna test ranges (a reflector makes a plane wave at short range) or by near-field scanning with a transform.
Level 3 — calibration, polarisation and draft-plan pitfalls
1. How the path-loss table is made. Put a reference antenna of known gain (a standard-gain horn) at the DUT position. Measure the transfer from the instrument port at every frequency, polarisation and (if the probe moves) angle. The table then holds "instrument port to isotropic point at the DUT". Any change of cable, probe, connector torque or chamber layout invalidates it. The draft plan also asks for a 15-minute settle after positioner moves (thermal drift) and a check that the positioner is in hold.

2. Polarisation. AAUs usually use ±45° dual-polarised elements. EIRP and EIS are defined for the total over two orthogonal polarisations. For power you measure both and power-sum them. For sensitivity you either drive a known polarisation and account for it, or use a dual-pol probe. Measuring only one linear polarisation against a slant element under-reads by up to about 3 dB.

3. TRP is not EIRP at boresight. TRP needs a sphere (or a standard-accepted reduced grid, or a beam-based approximation). One boresight point measures EIRP. The per-port "OTA output power" in the draft plan is really a path-loss-corrected power referred to the antenna port. That is useful for bring-up, but it is not a TRP or EIRP conformance number.

4. Ratios survive, sign conventions do not. ACLR measured OTA keeps its value, because path loss is flat to about 0.1 dB across ±2 BW and cancels in the ratio. But the draft plan's worked example concludes that −47.0 dBc fails a −45 dBc gate, calling more negative "worse". That is backwards. 47 dB of adjacent-channel suppression is better than 45 dB and passes. Always write ACLR as a positive ratio and compare magnitudes.

5. Treat the internal OTA plan as a draft. It still has TBDs: the OTA pass gates, positioner control commands and the per-antenna boresight table. In the middle of its RX example it even corrects itself after first computing an impossible +48.5 dBm SG level. The solid parts are the method, the formulas and the TDD SG gating. OTA uncertainty is larger than conducted, so the standards allow larger test tolerances (roughly 1–2 dB against ~0.7 dB conducted), and internal gates should not simply copy conducted ones.
Interview Q&A
Q: What is EIS and how do you measure it?
A: Equivalent isotropic sensitivity: the lowest power, referred to an ideal isotropic antenna at the DUT position, arriving from a given direction, at which the receiver still meets the reference throughput (BLER ≤ 5 %). You search the SG level down and subtract the calibrated path loss: EIS = SGmin − PathLoss(f, az, el).
Q: Your chamber path loss is 75 dB and the EIS target is −101.5 dBm. What SG level do you set?
A: SG = EIS_target + PathLoss = −101.5 + 75 = −26.5 dBm, re-evaluated for each frequency and angle because the path loss changes.
Q: EIRP vs TRP: when is each used?
A: EIRP is directional (per beam or direction) and is used for radiated transmit power declarations. TRP is the sphere-integrated total and is used for OTA output power and for unwanted emissions (ACLR, OBUE, spurious), where interference to others does not depend on one direction.
Q: Why does a 1.6 m AAU need a compact range or near-field system?
A: The far-field distance 2D²/λ is about 12 m at 700 MHz for D = 1.6 m. That is far beyond a normal anechoic chamber. A compact antenna test range makes a plane wave with a reflector at short distance. Near-field scanning measures close in and transforms the result to far field.
Q: An OTA report shows ACLR = −47 dBc marked FAIL against a −45 dBc limit. Comment.
A: The verdict logic is inverted. −47 dBc means the adjacent channel is 47 dB below the carrier, which is better than the 45 dB requirement, so it passes. Compare magnitudes of the ratio, and fix the comparison in the harness.
2G RCT on the FHGW
G2RUN01 2G on the FHGW — running guide: rctCfg / rctCmdList / vran2gconfig, TRX & slot mapping, L1/L2 start-up, UL signal catalogue & CRC checks RCT click to expand ▾
In plain English
Running 2G RCT on an FHGW means three XML files tell the PHY what to send and receive (which carrier on which antenna, which logical channel on which slot, how long to capture), then you start L1 and an RCT “L2” app on the BBU and read the CRC statistics. Most first-run failures are configuration, not RF.
Level 1 — the files and what each controls
File (in the PHY pod)Controls
rctCfg.xmlper-TRX carrier: <trxId> 0–3, <antennaPort>, <centerFrequencyHz>, <dlFrequencyHz> (offset = centre − DL frequency); a commented-out TRX is not transmitted; <ttiPrintPeriod> = how many TTIs the PHY captures
rctCmdList.xmlwhich logical channel goes on which time slot, users per TRX (ueIndex), UL antennas and RX diversity (mrcIrcMode, mrcIrcAntBmpSel)
vran2gconfig.xmlPHY settings: debug log level, RCT enable, TRX-to-antenna map
oammgrconfig.xmlfronthaul connection over the fibre port (ports / MACs)
l1appthe 2G PHY L1 application
Up to 4 TRX can be configured and spread across antennas. On RCT normally only the first RX antenna is used (MRC/IRC bitmap selects the ports).
Level 1 — slot / user mapping
TRXueIndex (users)Note
TRX00–7DL always fully occupied (carries control on TS0)
TRX18–15
TRX216–23
TRX324–31
all32transmit to every user; up to 31 traffic users with TS0 reserved for control
Level 2 — run it
# inside the PHY pod
cd /opt/pw/2gphy/2G_phy/
./run_l1app.sh 2,5,6,26,29,30      # core list; wait for: "Main Loop: L1APP_INIT Done"
# second terminal, same directory
./rctApp
phystart                            # live CRC / statistics start printing
Typical rctApp command sequence per test (from the trigger sheet): cellDelete → cellSetup true 0 0 1 0 80 70 70 70 70 10 … → tchSetup <ts> 0 <chanType> 0 <codec> DISABLE 0 → tchDlFpConfig <ts> 0 <MCS1|TCH_EFS|TCH_AFS|TCH_AHS> true 0 0 false false 0. For RACH the cell is set up with cellSetup false … and the channel on TS4.
Level 2 — UL signal catalogue (sensitivity tests)
Signal file (UL)Channel3GPP limit (dBm, BLER/FER)FHGW sens. (dBm)tchSetup / tchDlFpConfig
MCS1–3_swapped_zeros_f26.binEDGE MCS1–3−104, 10 %−82 … −82.5tchSetup 3 0 4 0 15 · tchDlFpConfig 3 0 MCS1
MCS4_swapped_zeros_f26.binEDGE MCS4−101.5, 10 %−81same

“FHGW sens.” is copied as recorded in the team’s sheet; the sheet does not state the reference plane, so compare codecs against each other rather than against the antenna-port limit. Static reference sensitivity procedure and pass rules: see G2SENS01.
Level 3 — expected CRC counts and quick checks
  • TCH: 24 CRCs per 104 frames (e.g. 416 TTIs → 96); SACCH: 1 per 104; RACH: 1 per frame (102 TTIs → 102 CRCs). Details: GSM01.
  • No statistics after phystart → L1 did not finish init or the fronthaul/oammgr config is wrong.
  • CRCs on the wrong slot or none on TRX1–3 → rctCmdList user mapping (ueIndex) or a commented TRX in rctCfg.
  • Sensitivity worse on one antenna → mrcIrcAntBmpSel / mrcIrcMode and the TRX-to-antenna map (the B8 two-antenna RCA in G2TX01 is the classic example).
Interview Q&A
Q: Which file decides which logical channel is on which time slot?
A: rctCmdList.xml — it also sets users per TRX and the MRC/IRC antenna selection.
Q: How many users can a 4-TRX 2G RCT setup address?
A: TRX0 users 0–7 … TRX3 users 24–31; ueIndex 32 means all. TS0 of TRX0 is reserved for control, so up to 31 traffic users.
Q: You captured 416 TTIs of TCH and saw 72 CRCs. What next?
A: Expected 96 (416/104×24). 72 means one 104-frame block missing or the capture was shorter — check ttiPrintPeriod and that the channel is mapped on the slot you think.
Q: How do you start a 2G RCT run on the BBU?
A: In the PHY pod run ./run_l1app.sh with the core list until “L1APP_INIT Done”, then ./rctApp in a second terminal and phystart.
Reading the rctApp statistics — a real output and what it tells you
==== PHY has already run for 55080 TTI (4.6154ms per TTI) ===
RACH:     Carrier [0], Time Slot [0], CRC Total [1080], CRC Pass [1080], CRC Fail [0]
          MAX/MIN/AVG RSSI [-3dBFs]   SNR [0dB]   TA [5]  (unit 1/4 symbol)
TCH/EFS:  Carrier [0], Time Slot [4], CRC Total [471],  CRC Pass [0],    CRC Fail [471]
          BER [10]  C2I [0]  RSSI [-3dBFs]  SNR [0dB]  TA [7]
SACCH/TF: Carrier [0], Time Slot [4], CRC Total [20],   CRC Pass [0],    CRC Fail [20]
          BER [10]  C2I [0]  RSSI [-3dBFs]  SNR [0dB]  TA [7]
FieldMeaningHealthy looks like
TTI (4.6154 ms)one GSM TDMA framekeeps counting while the test runs
Carrier / Time SlotTRX index and slot the channel is mapped tomatches rctCmdList (here RACH on TS0, traffic on TS4)
CRC Total / Pass / Faildecoded blocks and their CRC resultFail ≈ 0 at high level; fail rate = FER/BLER at the sensitivity point
RSSI [dBFS]received level at the ADC (full scale = 0 dBFS)well below 0 dBFS; −3 dBFS is near clipping
SNR, C2Isignal-to-noise and carrier-to-interference from the training sequenceclearly positive dB values
BERraw (pre-decoding) bit-error estimatelow
TAtiming advance estimate, in quarter-symbol units (1 symbol ≈ 3.69 µs)stable, small on a cabled bench
Reading this example (from the trigger spreadsheet): RACH on TS0 passes every CRC, but TCH/EFS and SACCH on TS4 fail every block, with BER at its ceiling, SNR and C/I at 0 dB and RSSI at −3 dBFS on every line. That pattern is not a sensitivity limit. It points to a setup problem: either the input is far too hot and the ADC is saturating (re-check the generator level and cable loss), or the traffic channel is not mapped where the signal is (slot/TRX/ueIndex in rctCmdList, or the codec in tchSetup / tchDlFpConfig doesn’t match the waveform). Rule of thumb: some channels pass and others fail at identical RSSI → configuration; everything degrades together as the level drops → real sensitivity.
Count check: 55 080 TTIs ÷ 51 = 1 080, so the RACH count here matches one access burst per 51-frame multiframe in this signal file. Always compute the expected count for the waveform you play (GSM01) before trusting a pass ratio.
RCT test-case map
RCTTC01 RCT Test Cases One by One — the 15 tests (volume · clarity · neighbours · ears), limits, real bench examples, confusion-busters & S-B-A-D triage RCT click to expand ▾
In plain English
Every RCT test answers one of four questions: Volume (am I as loud as promised, and can I control it?), Clarity (is my signal clean?), Neighbours (do I stay out of everyone else’s spectrum?) and Ears (can I hear phones correctly?). Tx tests: the EXM measures what the radio sends. Rx tests: the EXM generates a known signal and the RU/PHY reports what it heard. This card is the one-page map of all 15, with the limits and a real example for each.
Level 1 — the 15 tests and their limits
#TestQuestion it answersKey limit / expectation
1BS output powerVolumerated ±2 dB; rated B1/B3/B28 44.3 dBm, B8 43.1, B41 44.4 dBm (E-TM 1.1)
2ACLRNeighbours≥ 45 dB (3GPP), ≥ 44.2 dB with tolerance, ≥ 55 dB customer target; offsets ±1, ±2 channels
3EVM + frequency errorClarityQPSK 17.5 %, 16QAM 12.5 %, 64QAM 8 %, 256QAM 3.5 %; ±0.05 ppm
4SEM (OBUE)Neighboursstaircase mask to 10 MHz beyond the band edge, e.g. Cat B −7 → −14 dBm/100 kHz (0–5 MHz)
5SpuriousNeighboursCat B −36 dBm (< 1 GHz), −30 dBm/MHz (1–12.75 GHz); own UL band −96 dBm/100 kHz
6Occupied BWNeighbours99 % power inside the channel (≈ 18 MHz for 20 MHz)
7Tx dynamic rangeVolume5/10/15/20 MHz: 13.9 / 16.9 / 18.7 / 20 dB (no test tolerance)
8Reduced output powerVolumecommanded step ±2 dB, EVM/ACLR still pass (see RCOP01)
9CCDF / PAPRClarity≈ 8 dB at 0.01 % after CFR (raw OFDM ≈ 11 dB+)

12Reference sensitivityEars≥ 95 % throughput, e.g. wide area −101.5 dBm

14Rx dynamic rangeEarswanted e.g. −70.2 dBm + AWGN, ≥ 95 % throughput
15PRACH (planned)Earsdetection ≥ 99 %, false alarm ≤ 0.1 %
Level 2 — real examples from our benches (most failures are not the radio)
TestReal bench example → lesson
Output powerTx read 65 dB low: eAxC hard-coded to ANT A while ANT D was cabled → code fix. B3 swinging 41.6–46.4 dBm across nightlies (B1 steady) → DPD firmware suspected.
ACLRB3 54–57 dB in-band vs 55 dB target is marginal; 59–61 dB “passes” were outside the band, flattered by the filter. ACLR ≈ 0 with EVM ≈ 90 % = radio still on the previous band → measuring noise.
EVMB41 8.8 %: SSF 7 set in PHY and analyser but the RU didn’t follow → TDD switching misaligned. CI EVM 71 %: only a radio firmware change (DUC scaling).
SEMA narrow spur averages away in ACLR but fails SEM — read the worst-margin point; band edges are worst (filter skirt).
SpuriousB28 ~790 MHz × 2 ≈ 1580 MHz near GPS L1. On the ECS bench the E6640A has no spurious app → “−113 / 999 FAIL” is an equipment limit, not the radio.
OBW9 MHz OBW on a “20 MHz” test = RU really at 10 MHz; set_bandwidth reads the XML, not the RU.
Tx dynamic rangeB8 10 MHz 16.6–16.8 dB vs 16.9 → single RB 0.2–0.4 dB too hot (raised as a bug).
Reduced powerMeasured the generator instead of the analyser — both instruments were named “ant4”.
PA protectionB41 looked like a fail: sampled ~22 s late (blocked on NETCONF) and missed the 5 s hold → threaded → 3.087 dB PASS.
SensitivityApparent 10 dB shortfall: calibrated at DSA 0, applied at DSA 10; at DSA 0 → −108.7 dBm. B41 ~3.7 dB deficit + top-of-band roll-off still open.
RSSIOffset indexed by bus, not antenna letter; B28 needs two offsets; RSSI frozen at the noise floor when the wrong band was active.
PRACH“Not Tested” with SCPI −256: generator ARB memory wiped — the ARB is volatile, check :SOUR:RAD:ARB:CAT? before every run.
Level 3 — confusion-busters and failure triage
ACLRSEMSpurious
Wherenext channel (±1, ±2)just outside the channel, ≤ 10 MHz9 kHz – 12.75 GHz, far away
Howratio of channel powersevery point vs a staircase maskabsolute level vs a flat limit
Catchesbroad leakage (PA, DPD)narrow close-in spikesharmonics, clocks, mixing
UnitdB (relative)dBm / 100 kHzdBm / MHz
EVM vs ACLR: EVM = inside my channel (clarity); ACLR = outside it (neighbours). Sensitivity vs RSSI: can I decode a weak signal vs do I report the level right. Tx dynamic range vs reduced power: DR changes the load (RBs); ROP changes the commanded power.

S-B-A-D triage when a test fails — in this order:
  1. Setup — right band activated? right antenna / eAxC? instrument names unique? carriers ACTIVE?
  2. Bench — cabling, cable-loss table, RF switch position, EXM ARB loaded, PTP LOCKED?
  3. Automation — config/cadence honoured? sampling at the right time? known engine bug?
  4. Device — only now suspect the radio: firmware change, calibration, real HW fault.
Interview Q&A
Q: ACLR reads ≈ 0 dB and EVM ≈ 90 %. Radio broken?
A: Almost certainly not — the radio is still on the previous band (or the wrong port is measured), so the analyser sees noise. Check the active band/carrier first (S in S-B-A-D).
Q: Why can a signal pass ACLR but fail SEM?
A: ACLR averages power over a whole adjacent channel, so a narrow spur disappears in the average; SEM checks every point against a staircase mask and catches it.
Q: OBW shows 9 MHz on a 20 MHz test. What happened?
A: The RU is really running 10 MHz — the automation read the bandwidth from the XML, not from the running radio. Verify the running config.
Q: A 10 dB sensitivity shortfall appears after a DSA change. Why?
A: Calibration was done at one DSA setting and applied at another (e.g. DSA 0 vs 10); re-measuring at the calibrated DSA restores −108.7 dBm. Calibration constants are DSA- and image-dependent.
Q: What does S-B-A-D stand for?
A: Setup, Bench, Automation, Device — check them in that order; only suspect the radio once the first three are clean.
TX power, timing & CA tests
TXPWR01 RU Tx Power Control — one DAC current, many contributors (EEPROM freq/temp compensation, PA warm-up, Dynamic-Vdd LUT, thermal de-rating, ATE) RCT click to expand ▾
In plain English
An RU has many reasons to change its transmit power. The DU asks for a lower carrier gain, a cold PA needs a gentle start, the output drifts with frequency and temperature, an energy-saving feature drops the PA supply voltage, and a hot unit must back off. In the RU firmware all of these end in the same knob: the DAC output current (see DACG01), written through rfdc_write_current(). This card follows every contributor to that knob, shows how factory calibration data from EEPROM is turned into a current, and explains the newer rules (GRDEV-6571 power management, GRDEV-5664 graduated thermal de-rating) that decide who wins when several contributors want different things. If you remember one thing: one owner writes the DAC, everyone else asks it to. When a CLI poke or a second thread writes the DAC behind the owner's back, the next recompute silently overwrites it, or worse, an attenuation is never removed.
Six contributors, one owner, one register path
Target design from the power-management SRS: all contributors are funnelled through the Operations Manager, which alone calls the DAC write.
Level 1 — core facts
Who calls the DAC today. Three callers end in rfdc_write_current(): the Operations Manager on carrier activation (configure_all_dacs_and_wola() / configure_pa()), the System Monitor temperature thread, and the CLI. The power-management SRS keeps this structure and does not add a new process. It wraps every power setting in one API, and the System Monitor and CLI send IPC messages to the Operations Manager instead of writing the DAC themselves.

ContributorApplies toWhat it does
PA protectionallWARMUP state at reduced gain, then READY (immediate on Mini-Metro). See PAWARM01.
Frequency compensationMini-Metro, B41 (only if an RFFE cal table exists)Flattens output vs carrier frequency from EEPROM factory points.
Temperature compensationMini-Metro in software; AAU RFFE MCU does it internallygain_p_deg_db_per_c × (T_cal − T_now).
Reduced carrier powerMetro AAUScales DAC current from the M-plane carrier gain (see RCOP01).
Heat protection (legacy)allHIGH temperature adds 1 dB DAC attenuation; CRITICAL resets the FHGW. See THERM01.
Dynamic Vddwhen enabled per bandLowers PA drain voltage, compensates with pre-CFR and DAC gain (see PAE01).
Graduated de-rating (GRDEV-5664)when feature bit 1 set0.2 dB/°C above threshold, capped at 2.0 dB.

Percent conventions (GRDEV-6571). Carrier_Max = carrier Tx power (tx-array-carrier gain) as a percentage of the array maximum (tx-array max-gain): full power 100 %, −3 dB = 50 %, a deactivated carrier 0 %. PA_Max = the sum of Carrier_Max of all carriers on that PA, rounded up to the next 10 %. Rule of thumb in the SRS: powers coming from O-RAN stay in dB, derived quantities are in %, and attenuations are always in dB.

Factory compensation data (GRDEV-5996). Each DAC has a calibration temperature, a 7-point table of DAC current vs Tx power, and up to 70 frequency→power points (B41 uses 38 points across its 194 MHz band at 5 MHz spacing). The current is always clamped to 2250–40000 µA.
Level 2 — configure, test and measure
1. Boot path of the compensation data.
start_transmission.sh  configure_flavour()
  B41 models  : read FHGW EEPROM  (I2C 0x54, offset 2048, 3072 B = partition 2)
  other units : read RFFE EEPROM  (I2C 0x56, offset 0,    8192 B)
  -> minimetro_eeprom.py decode -> mini_metro_eeprom.json
operations_manager -> read_rf_eeprom_file() -> dacCalibrationInfo[]
B41 is detected at run time by is_band_41_supported (one band capability and that band is 41); this replaced a compile-time macro. The test plan lists different offsets for some models, so confirm the EEPROM source on the unit you are testing.

2. The compensation arithmetic.
P_avg      = linear mean of the cal points inside Fc +/- BW/2
power_delta = P(Fc) - P_avg                       # frequency flatness
base_I      = interpolate(current-vs-power table, target_power_dbm)
temp_delta  = gain_p_deg_db_per_c * (T_cal - T_now)
I_final     = base_I * 10^((power_delta - temp_delta)/20)   clamp 2250..40000 uA
Compensation is applied in WARMUP and on the first READY pass. Mini-Metro then re-applies it every 10th loop iteration; on the AAU the RFFE MCU handles temperature itself.

3. Dynamic-Vdd personality parameters (per band).
ParameterRange / defaultMeaning
Adjust_PA_voltage_with_carrier_powerTRUE/FALSE, default FALSEEnable Vdd tracking of PA_Max
Adjust_PA_voltage_step_period_sec1–60 s, default 5Pause between LUT steps
LUT entry: PA_Vdd0–60 VDrain voltage for this step
LUT entry: CFR_gain0–511, default 215Pre-CFR gain (DL_DFE_CFR_GAIN) to keep CFR at its working point
LUT entry: DAC_gain0–6 dBDAC gain relative to the carrier-gain operating point
LUT entry: PA_Max10–100 %Highest PA_Max this entry can support
Example LUT from the SRS: 16 entries from 40 V down to 25 V in 1 V steps, CFR_gain 215 → 155 (−4 per step) and DAC_gain 0 → 1.5 dB, used when PA_Max ≤ 50 %. The RU walks one entry at a time, waiting the step period between entries, until it reaches the lowest Vdd that still supports the target PA_Max.

4. What to grep while testing.
grep -E 'rffe_eeprom|read_rf_eeprom'        fhgw.log   # which EEPROM was decoded
grep -E 'WARMUP|READY'                      fhgw.log   # PA state machine
grep -E 'dac_current|power_delta|temp_delta' fhgw.log   # the numbers actually used
5. De-rating test plan worth copying: a 1 °C-step sweep of the whole curve (check rounding at the x.x5 midpoints); sensor-exclusion tests (FPGA/SFP/midboard sensors must not trigger it); band independence on a two-band personality; composition against ATE attenuation and Dynamic Vdd; an on-target heat/release run; the negative case with the enable bit clear; a dropped request corrected on the next poll; upgrade and downgrade behaviour.
Level 3 — expert detail, pitfalls, real cases
Graduated de-rating (GRDEV-5664). The old protection was a fixed, edge-triggered 1 dB step. The new curve is 0.2 dB per °C above the threshold, rounded to 0.1 dB, capped at 2.0 dB (reached at +10 °C). Thresholds: AAU (Integrity-ME) 105 °C, Mini-Metro 85 °C, against High-Warning/Critical alarms of 110/120 °C (AAU) and 100/110 °C (MM). Only RFFE temperature channels count; each band is judged on its own RFFEs (band = slot ÷ RFFEs-per-band, the same mapping as EPE PM, see CM21). A band with no readable RFFE gets no de-rating, and no other band's reading is borrowed. It is recomputed on every temperature poll (60 s on all shipped personalities), so the response is a staircase with no latch and no hysteresis; a lost request self-corrects on the next poll.

Composition rules. Attenuations with different reasons take the maximum (de-rating vs ATE). De-rating is additive on top of the Dynamic-Vdd gain, never a replacement. Writing a de-rating of 0 clears only the high-temperature slot.

Pitfalls and real cases.
• Attenuation that never clears: the legacy 1 dB HIGH-temperature step was not always removed when the alarm cleared (GRDEV-6571-100 → GRDEV-7180). The unit then ran 1 dB low for no visible reason. This is exactly the failure that a single owner with per-reason slots prevents.
• PSU is the Vdd bottleneck: the POC found that Vdd takes 5–10 s to settle per step, so one big step makes the output droop or overshoot. Measured 48 V → 35 V moved Tx from 46.1 to 44.1 dBm, about 0.1–0.2 dB per 1 V step, which is why the design uses 1 V steps with a digital-gain correction at each one.
• Calibration vs power saving: ATE calibration with set-atten-dfe <dac> <index> <atten in 0.1 dB> must be refused while any power-saving feature can move the PA level (GRDEV-6571-400). Newer builds replace that command with set-dac-atten (see DACG01).
• Feature-bit traps: de-rating is enabled by bit 1 of the pw-aau-features bitmap (bit 0 is uSleep, default 0). A unit upgraded to this release loses the old 1 dB protection until the EMS sets bit 1; after a downgrade with bit 1 still set, the old image refuses the startup-config replay.
• Two thermal tables: the older compensation overview quotes 85 °C → −1 dB on all DACs and 105 °C → all DACs off. The de-rating SRS uses the per-platform thresholds above. Check which scheme the image under test implements before writing limits.
• EEPROM failures: a missing or malformed EEPROM JSON raises an EEPROM-file alarm and the unit carries on without compensation (power error up to the raw flatness); a carrier outside the calibrated range raises a configuration error.
Interview Q&A
Q: Why route every power contributor through one owner instead of letting each module write the DAC?
A: Because the DAC current is one shared value. If the temperature thread and the carrier path both write it, the last writer wins and an attenuation can be lost or never removed (the GRDEV-7180 bug). One owner keeps a slot per reason and composes them deterministically.
Q: Two carriers on one PA are set to −3 dB and −6 dB below the array maximum. What is PA_Max?
A: Carrier_Max is 50 % and 25 % (−3 dB halves the power, −6 dB quarters it). The sum is 75 %, rounded up to the next 10 %, so PA_Max = 80 %. A deactivated carrier would contribute 0 %.
Q: How does the RU convert a frequency and temperature correction into DAC current?
A: It computes power_delta = P(Fc) minus the linear mean of the calibration points in the carrier bandwidth, temp_delta = gain-per-°C × (T_cal − T_now), and scales the interpolated base current by 10^((power_delta − temp_delta)/20), then clamps to 2250–40000 µA.
Q: The unit is 4.3 °C over its de-rating threshold. How much attenuation, and what if the ATE attenuation is 0.5 dB?
A: 0.2 × 4.3 = 0.86, rounded to 0.9 dB. ATE and de-rating are different reasons, so the larger one wins: 0.9 dB.
Q: Why lower Vdd in 1 V steps instead of one jump?
A: The PSU needs 5–10 s to settle, so a big step causes a power droop or overshoot. 1 V steps change output by only 0.1–0.2 dB and the firmware corrects the digital gain at each step, keeping the transient error small.
NTA01 N_TA,offset on the B41 TDD FHGW — the ul-delay register, the 245.76 MHz tick, why TA read 4 and why the first fix cut throughput (GRDEV-5757) RCT click to expand ▾
In plain English
In TDD the UE starts its uplink a little earlier than the downlink timing says, by a fixed amount called NTA,offset (about 20 µs for LTE TDD). That gives the radio time to switch from transmit to receive. The RU must open its uplink sampling window at the matching instant. On the B41 TDD FHGW that instant is one raw FPGA counter value, ul-delay. If it is a few hundred ticks off, the base station measures a non-zero timing advance (TA = 4) on a UE sitting on a short cable next to the radio, as if the UE were 300 m away. Nothing breaks because the cyclic prefix hides the error, but the maximum cell range shrinks. This card (GRDEV-5757) shows how to turn microseconds into register ticks in the right clock domain, why the first fix overshot and cut throughput, and where the value lives.
The three ul-delay values on the B41 TDD personality
Each step of 128 ticks moves the measured TA by one; the reverted value overshot the optimum by about 2 TA.
Level 1 — core facts
Code path. lphy_config.json → personality lphy-config.ul-delay (uint32) → set_sync_delay() → FPGA register UL_SYNC_RX_DELAY_B(0), written raw with no scaling. The register has two instances (band 0/1) but only B(0) is written. The O-RAN nta-offset-value in ru-compliance is used only for M-plane validation and never reaches the FPGA, so changing it in the YANG does nothing to the real timing.

Carrier typeCounter clock1 tick10 ms frame
LTE, NR 15 kHz245.76 MHz4.069 ns2,457,600 ticks
NR 30 kHz491.52 MHz2.035 ns4,915,200 ticks
(not this register) TDD switching domain122.88 MHz8.14 ns1,228,800 (TDD_MAX_FRAME_OFFSET)
The counter ticks in the carrier sample-clock domain, not the TDD-switching domain. An early analysis used 122.88 MHz and was wrong by a factor of two.

The B41 carrier is LTE TDD, 20 MHz, 100 PRB at 15 kHz, so the 245.76 MHz domain applies. ul-delay is one scalar for the whole carrier, not split per SCS.
Conversion: 1 TA = 16 Ts = 128 ticks at 245.76 MHz (≈ 0.52 µs).
Level 2 — how to calculate, change and test
Converting a timing error into a register change
error_us   = TA_measured * 0.5208          # 1 TA = 16 Ts = 0.5208 us (LTE)
ticks      = error_us * 245.76             # LTE / NR 15 kHz carriers
ticks      = error_us * 491.52             # NR 30 kHz carriers
TA 4       -> about 2.08 us -> about 512 ticks (measured optimum: +492)
new value  = 2,452,659 + 492 = 2,453,151  -> PRACH TA reads 0
Three independent cross-checks that 245.76 MHz is right: a calibration note of 4915 cycles = 20 µs; the shipped B41 value 2,452,659 = frame − 4,941 ticks ≈ 20.1 µs (the LTE TDD NTA,offset); and an n78 value of 4,909,374 that only gives the expected 11.85 µs at 491.52 MHz.

How to verify on the bench. Put a UE (or a PRACH generator) on a short cable, read the PRACH-detected TA in the PHY log, change ul-delay in steps of 128 ticks and confirm TA moves by one per step. Then run a UL throughput test (see PRA01 for PRACH detection and L21 for UL timing) at the chosen value, because TA = 0 alone does not prove the sampling window is centred.

Where to edit. On develop the value lives in two real personality JSONs (the n41 -00-2 and -01-2 models). The B41 model names are git symlinks to them and pick up the change automatically. Only the TDD variants carry 2,452,659 (4 of the 12 B41-capable model names); the other 8 use ul-delay = 610.
Level 3 — expert detail and pitfalls
Why TA = 4 caused no KPI loss. The B41 personality uses a CP of 144 Ts ≈ 4.69 µs. A 2 µs early/late sampling error stays inside the CP, so orthogonality is kept and BLER is unaffected. The cost is range: the base station believes every UE is already 4 TA away, so the usable TA budget, and therefore the maximum cell radius, shrinks.

Why the first fix was reverted. It set 2,453,428 (+769 ticks = +3.13 µs ≈ 6 TA). TA did go to zero, but the window was now about 2 TA past the optimum, which shifted the UL sampling window too early relative to the arriving symbols and used up the CP margin on the other side and cutting throughput. Lesson: a TA readout that clamps at 0 cannot tell you that you overshot. Always confirm with a throughput or EVM measurement, and prefer the value that centres the window (+492).

Windows checkout trap. On Windows a git symlink is checked out as a 40-byte text file that contains the target path. Editing or overwriting it turns the symlink into a regular file, and the B41 model silently stops following the n41 file.

General rule. A PRACH-measured TA that stays non-zero on a short cable means the RU's UL timing reference is offset. Before touching any register, work out which clock domain the counter runs in (sample clock vs TDD switching vs frame-offset) and convert µs to ticks there. The same mistake also shows up in TDD trigger-delay setups on the signal generator (see B41T).
Interview Q&A
Q: What is N_TA,offset and why does TDD need it?
A: A fixed advance of the UE uplink relative to the downlink timing (624 Ts ≈ 20.3 µs in LTE TDD). It gives the base station time to switch from TX to RX. The RU must open its UL window to match, otherwise every UE appears to have a timing error.
Q: Your UE on a 1 m cable reports TA = 4. What do you suspect and how do you fix it?
A: An offset in the RU's UL timing reference, not real distance. 4 TA ≈ 2.08 µs; at 245.76 MHz that is about 512 ticks. Step ul-delay in 128-tick increments until TA reaches 0, then confirm throughput; on B41 the optimum was +492 ticks.
Q: Why did someone get the conversion wrong by ×2?
A: They used the 122.88 MHz TDD-switching clock. The ul-delay counter runs in the 245.76 MHz carrier sample clock for LTE/NR 15 kHz (491.52 MHz for NR 30 kHz).
Q: Changing nta-offset-value over NETCONF did nothing. Why?
A: In this implementation that leaf is only used for M-plane validation. The FPGA uses the personality ul-delay value written by set_sync_delay().
Q: Why did the reverted fix still read TA = 0 but lose throughput?
A: It overshot by about 2 TA. TA reporting cannot go below zero, so the overshoot was hidden, but the sampling window moved too early and the CP margin was used up.
TMRCT01 FHGW tmRCT — running 4G RCT tests from the enb_app console (configure.sh, test IDs, PRACH re-offset, 2-cell tests, limits) RCT click to expand ▾
In plain English
tmRCT is a way to run 4G conformance-style RCT tests (E-TM downlink, FRC uplink, PRACH) against an FHGW without a full LTE stack. A single program, enb_app, runs the PHY, the O-RAN 7.2 fronthaul and the canned test vectors in one process on the DU. You start it, wait for its console, type a test ID, and the radio transmits a 3GPP test model or listens for a known uplink waveform from the signal generator. The DU install, model flash, firmware upgrade, PTP and NETCONF activation are covered in OPS3; this card is only the tmRCT part: the packages, configure.sh, the test-ID map, two-cell tests, the FHGW limits and the usual reasons a test produces nothing. For the automated equivalent and the ruauto rctdl map see FWK5.
tmRCT setup
Downlink is measured on the analyser; uplink tests decode a waveform injected by the signal generator.
Level 1 — core facts
Packages. Two archives are needed and must come from the same build folder: generic-4g-phy-<build>.release_x86_ubuntu2204.tgz and tmrct_tests.tgz. Extract both into one staging folder inside the phynode container and check that bin/lte/l1/enb_app and submodules/tv/testmac exist. Mismatched packages fail when loading tests with an iguana error: expected [pa]… parse message.

Console test types: rctdl, rctul, rctfd (FDD, UL on cell 0 + DL on cell 1), rctdl_tdd, rctul_tdd. Bandwidths 5, 10, 15, 20 MHz.

TestTest IDsNotes
DL E-TM, 1 cell6111 … 6119E-TM1.1, 1.2, 2, 3.1, 3.2, 3.3, 3.1a, 2a, 1.4 in that order
UL FRC A1-3, FDD31 / 61 / 81 (1/2/4 ant)+4 = bidirectional "+DL" variant (35/65/85). No 5 MHz A1-3 test.
UL FRC A1-3, TDD13000 / 16000 / 18000+1 = +DL; RB offset adds 250/500/750
PRACH format 0, FDD39 (1 ant; 45 at 15 MHz), 669 (2 ant), 679 (4 ant)Generator PRACH offset must match the personality re-offset
PRACH, TDD130001 / 130002PRACH config index 4 only
DL, 2 cells6211; 622x6211 = E-TM1.1 on both; 622x = E-TMx on cell 0 with E-TM1.1 on cell 1
UL, 2 cellsu rctul 231A1-3 on both cells; UL is always measured on cell 0 (B1 in dual band)
UL+DL mixedrctfd 659/669/679, 6352…PRACH or A1-3 on cell 0 with E-TM1.1 on cell 1
FHGW limits. Maximum 1cc output: B1 −16.7 dBm, B3 −17.0 dBm, B41 −23 dBm; with 2cc each carrier is 3 dB lower (−19.7 / −20.0 dBm). Sensitivity point −69 dBm (B1/B3). TDD: frame config 2, special subframe 6, PRACH config index 4, one cell only. At most 2 bands × 2 carriers and bands × carriers × antennas ≤ 16.
Level 2 — configure and run
1. Configure. From the PHY folder, ./configure.sh <bands> <cc> [band_id] writes oammgrconfig.xml, param_enb.json and selects the three libraries (libxran, libicc, libwls) in one go.
ArgumentsResult
1 11 band, 1 carrier
1 21 band, 2 carriers
2 1dual band, 1 carrier each
2 24 cells
2 1,23 cells
band_idB1/B3 board: 0 = B1, 1 = B3. B41 uses 0
Environment overrides: ANTS=2, DUPLEX=tdd (TDD only allows 1 1), CARRIER_OFFSET=1 (LTE on RU carrier 1 for MSR, where carrier 0 is 2G), RU_MAC, PHYNODE, L1RT_CORES.

2. Personality re-offset for PRACH (in the RU personality JSON, non-CA values; reboot after editing):
BWFDD PRACH offset / re-offsetTDD (B41) PRACH offset / re-offset
5 MHz14 / 128414 / 1284
10 MHz35 / 373237 / 4308
15 MHz59 / 704462 / 7908
20 MHz83 / 1035686 / 11220
3. Activate the carriers over NETCONF after every RU reboot (see OPS3). An inactive carrier gives no RF at all.

4. Run.
cd bin/lte/l1
LD_LIBRARY_PATH=. ./enb_app tmrct param_enb.json
# wait for: Welcome to the Application Console  (anything typed earlier is ignored)
u rctdl 6111 20      # E-TM1.1, 20 MHz
u rctul 31 20        # FRC A1-3, 1 antenna
u rctul 39 20        # PRACH format 0
f my_list.json       # run a list of tests
tm-exit              # stop
# live switching (needs PW_TMRCT_LIVE_SWITCH=1):  n  = next test,  ant <eaxc> = switch antenna
5. Verify DL power on the FHGW per antenna with power-monitor <path><ant> dl: path 0/1 = band 0 carrier 0/1, path 2/3 = band 1 carrier 0/1 (e.g. for i in 0 1 2 3; do power-monitor 0$i dl; done).

Manual equivalent of configure.sh (useful when the script does not fit your server): with T cores, the hyper-thread sibling of core c is c+T; nonRt uses 2 and 2+T; l1Rt uses two adjacent free cores plus their siblings (e.g. 3,4,35,36 when T = 32). In oammgrconfig.xml rename the <oran-spl8> block to <oran-spl7.2> and enable one <fhIf><inst> per cell. In param_enb.json, disabled cells get band_sector_id / carr_id = 4294967295, and siso_mode_copy_tx_to_bit_map_hw_ant is 15 for 4 antennas and 3 for 2.
Level 3 — troubleshooting and pitfalls
Troubleshooting map
SymptomUsual cause
No RF output at allCarrier not activated after reboot, wrong o-du-mac-address in the startup config, or wrong ruMac/cuMac in the PHY config
Only one band transmitsband_sector_id / carr_id wrong in param_enb.json
"numCells N but the application runs M cell(s)"Test cell count does not match configure.sh (e.g. a 62xx test on a 1-cell setup)
iguana error: expected [pa]…tmrct_tests.tgz from a different build than the PHY
PRACH never detectedre-offset does not match duplex/BW, or the generator PRACH offset differs
B41: no UL after a TX-only runRe-activate the carriers (or reboot the RU)
Commands ignored at startTyped before the console banner appeared
Known B41 issues. GRDEV-5757: the NTA,offset setting makes PRACH report TA = 4 (explained in NTA01). GRDEV-6218: CQI and DL throughput drop at the top of the band (EARFCN 41390), although DL throughput still passes the KPI.

Reading the limits correctly. The FHGW alone is a low-power test head: the −16.7 dBm and −69 dBm figures are FHGW-port values, not rated RU output or REFSENS. Use them as pass/fail sanity for the fronthaul and PHY path, not as 3GPP conformance numbers. In 2cc the two carriers share the power, so expect exactly 3 dB less per carrier; a different drop points to the gain split (see DACG01, PSPLIT01).
Interview Q&A
Q: What does tmRCT replace compared with a normal DU test setup?
A: The MAC, RRC and UE. enb_app runs PHY, fronthaul and pre-built test vectors in one process, so you can drive E-TM, FRC and PRACH tests through an FHGW with only a DU, an analyser and a generator.
Q: PRACH test 39 at 20 MHz FDD never detects. What do you check first?
A: That the personality re-offset is 10356 on all antennas and the generator's PRACH offset is 83, and that the carriers were re-activated after the last reboot.
Q: You configured '1 1' and ran u rctdl 6211. What happens?
A: It fails with a numCells mismatch: 6211 is a 2-cell test (E-TM1.1 on both cells) and needs a 2-cell configure.sh setup.
Q: Why does each carrier read 3 dB lower in a 2cc run?
A: Both carriers share the RU's total power budget equally, so each gets half (−3 dB). This is the equal-power split; see PSPLIT01 for equal-PSD splits with unequal bandwidths.
Q: Which cell is measured for UL in a dual-band 2-cell test?
A: Always cell 0, which is B1 in a B1/B3 dual-band setup.
IMD2CC01 2CC in-band spur debug — IMD3 vs I/Q image vs alias: classify by frequency and slope, isolate, fix (b0103 B1/B3) RCT click to expand ▾
In plain English
You enable the second carrier in a band for the first time and a spur appears inside the band. It could be three very different things: intermodulation (the PA or DAC is non-linear and mixes the two carriers), an I/Q image (the quadrature path is unbalanced and mirrors a carrier around the NCO), or an alias (a sampling-rate or NCO frequency-plan artefact). Each has a different fix, and backing off the power only cures the first one. This card gives a quick way to tell them apart from the spur's frequency and its slope when you change the level, then lists the usual software suspects on the b0103 (B1/B3) AAU, how to tell a real spur from an observation-path artefact, and the isolation procedure. Background on 2CC itself is in CA2CC01; on the DAC current in DACG01.
Where each spur type lands
IMD3 products sit one carrier spacing outside the pair; an image mirrors around the NCO; an alias follows the DAC/ADC sample rates.
Level 1 — core facts
b0103 layout. 8 DACs and 2 DPD tiles; the midboard splits each DAC to 4 PAs, 32 PAs in total. B1 uses DAC/ADC 0, 1, 4, 5 with NCO ≈ 2.14 GHz; B3 uses 2, 3, 6, 7 with NCO ≈ 1.8425 GHz. The observation receiver (ORX) is on ADC 8–9, one per DPD tile, time-multiplexed over 4 TX channels. Two CCs in the same band share one DAC (cc_id is deliberately not used in DAC selection). PAs are not shared across bands.

2CC headroom. b0103 is a high-power, non-5-band AAU, so each CC's gain must stay within MAX_POWER_2CC_GAIN = 3.0 dB (+0.05 dB tolerance) of the array maximum.

Spur classWhere it isLevel-sweep signatureFix domain
IMD3 (analog nonlinearity)2f1−f2 and 2f2−f1drops ~3 dB per 1 dB back-offoperating point: gain back-off, DAC current, DPD
I/Q image (QMC)mirror of a CC around the NCO; invisible with 1CC at band centredrops 1:1quadrature correction
Alias / foldingexplained by DAC 4.9152 GSPS images, ADC 2.4576 GSPS (×10 decimation) folding, or a wrong NCO worddrops 1:1frequency plan / digital config
The I/Q-image case is why a first 2CC test is so often where a latent quadrature problem shows up: with one carrier at band centre the image falls on top of the carrier itself and cannot be seen.
Level 2 — how to isolate and measure
Isolation procedure
1. One CC at a time: CC1 alone, CC2 alone, then both. A spur only with both is intermod. A spur with a single off-centre CC at its mirror around the NCO is an image.
2. Level sweep: back off 1 dB with set-dac-atten and watch the spur: ~3 dB drop = IMD3, 1:1 = image/alias.
3. Two-tone CW: arm_cw_playback <dac> <freq-offset> <amplitude> (continuous by default, stop_cw_playback to end) places clean tones at the two CC offsets for a textbook IMD3 reading.
4. IQ capture: record the ADC (reco_en / reco_ant_num) and FFT offline to get the exact spur frequency, then do the arithmetic against the table above.
5. After a fix re-adapt DPD on the 2CC composite and re-check ACLR and EVM (see ACLREVM01).

ToolUseCaveat
set-dac-atten / get-dac-attenTX level sweepGoes via operations_manager; needs an active carrier; rejected if Dynamic Vdd owns the DAC
set-dac-currentDirect DAC VOP poke on the benchBypasses the tx_power owner, overwritten on reconfigure
set-pre-cfr-gain <cc> <gain>Per-CC CFR headroomBypasses the owner, overwritten on carrier reconfiguration
set-adc-atten <adc> <0.1 dB>Rx / ORX DSAQuantised to the silicon step
get-rssiPer-ADC input leveldBm reading depends on adc_dbfs_adj matching the DSA
dpd_orx_manual_mode / _ch / _update, dpd_orx_nco_pausePin the ORX to one TX channel, freeze NCO switchingRegisters in the DL DFE map
dpd_orx_fsm_state / dpd_orx_chCheck ORX multiplexing is aliveStuck FSM: assert dpd_orx_init
Level 3 — suspects, artefacts and pitfalls
Top software suspects for a first-ever 2CC run
• DAC current "last-CC-wins". At the time of the debug guide, dac_current_compose_uA() was the single integration point for the 2CC combine, but the composed current was just the single-carrier value of whichever CC wrote last. Two CCs then push ~3 dB more composite power into an operating point sized for one, overdriving DAC/PA and creating real IMD. The shared-backoff algorithm (GRDEV-7873) replaces this; see DACG01.
• 2CC gain back-off not applied: each CC left at single-carrier max instead of within the 3 dB headroom.
• CFR overload is a level problem, not a PAPR problem. Two OFDM carriers have about the same PAPR as one, but the composite runs ~3 dB hotter into a clip threshold sized for 1CC, so CFR clips far more often and the clipping noise looks like in-band distortion. Fix the per-CC pre-CFR gain.
• DPD adapted on a bad observation: a diverged DPD gives regrowth that reads as IMD. Check that dpd_orx_fsm_state is cycling and the ORX levels are sane, then reload coefficients.

Spur only in the OBS capture? First prove it at the coupler or antenna port with a spectrum analyser. If it is absent there it is an observation artefact: ORX ADC overload from the +3 dB composite (add ORX attenuation), a DPD NCO register still holding a single-CC centre instead of the band centre (b0103 defaults 2.14 / 1.8425 GHz), or ORX multiplex mixing (pin one channel).

Spur in the main Rx? Check per-ADC get-rssi (B1 = ADC 0,1,4,5; B3 = 2,3,6,7), try LNA2 bypass (~15 dB less gain) and the ADC DSA. Also do the TX→RX leakage arithmetic: 2f1−f2 can land in the UL band for some placements (duplex spacing B1 190 MHz, B3 95 MHz). If the Rx spur vanishes with TX muted, it is the LNA/ADC intermodulating leaked DL.

Two things that are not spur mechanisms but surprise people: with intra-band 2CC, symbol micro-sleep is force-disabled in software (log: PL micro-sleep force-disabled, see USLEEP01); and because PAs are not shared across bands on b0103, a B1×B3 cross product points to coupling or receiver nonlinearity, never shared-PA IMD.
Interview Q&A
Q: A spur appears at 2f1−f2 when you turn on the second carrier. How do you prove it is real IMD3?
A: Back the drive off by 1 dB. Third-order IMD falls about 3 dB (3:1 slope); an image or alias falls 1:1. Confirm with CC1-only/CC2-only runs and a two-tone CW test.
Q: Why can a QMC problem stay hidden until the first 2CC test?
A: With one carrier at band centre on the NCO, its I/Q image mirrors onto itself. An off-centre CC in 2CC moves the image to an empty part of the band where it becomes visible.
Q: Why does CFR clip more in 2CC if the PAPR barely changes?
A: Because the composite level is ~3 dB higher while the clip threshold was sized for one carrier. It is a headroom problem; reduce the per-CC pre-CFR gain.
Q: The spur is in the DPD observation capture but not on the analyser. What now?
A: It is an observation artefact: ORX ADC overload, a DPD NCO still at a single-CC centre, or ORX channel multiplexing. Add ORX attenuation, check the NCO, pin the ORX to one channel.
Q: Why is a CLI fix with set-pre-cfr-gain not a real fix?
A: It bypasses the tx_power owner and is overwritten the next time the carrier is reconfigured. Use it to prove the cause, then fix the operating point in the owner path.
PSPLIT01 Two-carrier power split — equal power vs equal PSD, N_RB not MHz, NR examples, mixed SCS and the RU continuous-gain requirements RCT click to expand ▾
In plain English
When two carriers share one PA, they share one power budget X (the linear sum of both). There are two sensible ways to split it. Equal power gives each carrier half (X − 3.01 dB) whatever its bandwidth. Equal PSD gives each carrier power in proportion to its number of resource blocks, so the power per resource element (EPRE) is the same on both. Equal PSD makes RSRP, cell edge and reselection match between the carriers; equal power quietly gives the narrow carrier a coverage advantage. 3GPP conformance tests for multi-carrier (TS 38.141-1 NRTC1/2/3) require equal PSD, so the habit of a flat −3 dB split is wrong whenever the two bandwidths differ. This card shows the formula, the NR pitfall (split on N_RB, never MHz), mixed numerology, and what the RU must support so the DU can ask for any split.
Same total power, two shapes
Box area = carrier power, box height = PSD. LTE 5 MHz = 25 RB, 20 MHz = 100 RB.
Level 1 — core facts
Formulas
equal power :  P_i = X - 3.01 dB
equal PSD   :  P_i = X + 10*log10( N_RB,i / (N_RB,1 + N_RB,2) )
PSD advantage of the narrow carrier under equal power = 10*log10(N_RB,wide / N_RB,narrow)
   LTE 5 + 20 MHz: 10*log10(100/25) = 6.02 dB
Always split on N_RB, never on MHz. In LTE 25/50/75/100 RB scale exactly with 5/10/15/20 MHz, so MHz works by accident. NR does not scale linearly: at 15 kHz, 10 MHz = 52 RB and 20 MHz = 106 RB; at 30 kHz, 100 MHz = 273 RB. Using MHz ratios in NR gives errors up to about 0.25 dB.

LTE pairEqual powerEqual PSD (narrow / wide)
5 + 20 MHzX−3.01 / X−3.01X−6.99 / X−0.97
10 + 20 MHzX−3.01 / X−3.01X−4.77 / X−1.76
15 + 20 MHzX−3.01 / X−3.01X−3.68 / X−2.43
20 + 20 MHzX−3.01 / X−3.01X−3.01 / X−3.01
NR at 46 dBm joint power (equal PSD, narrow / wide): 15 kHz 10+20 → 41.2 / 44.3 dBm; 15 kHz 40+50 → 42.5 / 43.4 dBm; 30 kHz 20+100 → 38.0 / 45.3 dBm; 30 kHz 40+100 → 40.5 / 44.6 dBm. Note the last two: the wide carrier needs almost the whole budget on its own, so check the per-carrier PA rating, not just the total.
Level 2 — configure and measure
How to set up a 2CC power test
1. Get N_RB for each carrier from the bandwidth and SCS (TS 38.104 / 36.104 tables), not from MHz.
2. Decide the policy: conformance (NRTC1/2/3, ETC1/2/3) needs equal PSD with the sum equal to the rated total power; field configurations often use equal power because the per-carrier power cap is the knob operators actually turn.
3. Compute each carrier's power with the formula and convert to the per-carrier gain the DU will send over the M-plane (see DACG01 for how the RU maps gains onto DAC current and digital attenuation).
4. Measure each carrier's channel power and check that the linear sum equals the joint target, and that the EPRE (power ÷ N_RB ÷ 12) matches between carriers.

Worked conformance example (n78 40 + 50 MHz, 30 kHz). N_RB = 106 and 133. Equal PSD gives the 50 MHz carrier 10·log10(133/239) = −2.55 dB and the 40 MHz carrier −3.54 dB relative to the joint power: they differ by about 1 dB (≈0.97 dB if you use the MHz ratio 50/40). A flat −3 dB split is right for 40+40 and 50+50 but wrong for 40+50 / 50+40 (see CA2CC02).

NR power parameters. NR power is anchored on ss-PBCH-BlockPower (SSS EPRE in dBm per RE). powerControlOffsetSS sets CSI-RS relative to SSB and powerControlOffset sets PDSCH relative to CSI-RS. That decouples coverage from data power density: you can hold SSB EPRE identical on both carriers (same RSRP and cell edge) while the total power is split by N_RB.

Mixed SCS. Equal EPRE across a 15 kHz and a 30 kHz carrier is not equal PSD: the 30 kHz RE is twice as wide, so the 30 kHz carrier is 3 dB lower in dBm/Hz and about 3 dB worse in SNR per RE. To equalise link budget add 10·log10(SCS_B / SCS_A) to the wider-SCS carrier's EPRE. With the same SCS on both, EPRE and dBm/Hz are interchangeable and the tables above apply directly.
Level 3 — RU requirements, refarming and pitfalls
RU requirements for 2CC (RRH-manager SRS).
• The RU publishes both maximum and minimum power per antenna in its capabilities YANG (and in the per-model JSON).
• It must accept any continuous gain between min and max for up to 2 CCs per band, not a discrete set such as {20, 17} dB. A 2G carrier counts as a carrier; NB-IoT gets no special case.
• If disabling or re-enabling one carrier would drive the band below its minimum, the RU keeps transmitting the surviving carrier and raises TX-out-of-order (MAJOR) plus a configuration fault sourced to the carrier gain.
• On the BBU side the RRH manager stores per-band max/min Tx power in its database and fills 0.0 dBm when the RU does not publish them, which is a classic source of a nonsense power range in the GUI.

LTE → NR refarming. At the same nominal bandwidth NR has more RBs (10 MHz: 52 vs 50; 15 MHz: 79 vs 75; 20 MHz: 106 vs 100; only 5 MHz matches at 25). The resulting split offsets differ by less than 0.2 dB (e.g. 5+20: LTE −6.99/−0.97 vs NR −7.19/−0.92), which does not move a link budget, but does matter when an LTE and an NR carrier share one PA (DSS) and their EPRE must truly match: compute from real RB counts on both sides.

Pitfalls. Splitting on MHz in NR; assuming −3 dB per carrier in a conformance plan with unequal bandwidths; forgetting that the wide carrier under equal PSD may exceed the per-carrier PA rating; and comparing dBm/Hz across different numerologies as if they were EPRE.
Interview Q&A
Q: Joint power is 46 dBm, carriers are LTE 10 MHz and 20 MHz. What are the equal-PSD powers?
A: N_RB 50 and 100, so the 10 MHz carrier gets 46 + 10·log10(50/150) = 41.2 dBm and the 20 MHz carrier 46 + 10·log10(100/150) = 44.2 dBm. In NR at 15 kHz (52 and 106 RB) it becomes 41.2 / 44.3 dBm.
Q: Why not use the MHz ratio in NR?
A: NR RB counts are not proportional to bandwidth (20 MHz = 106 RB at 15 kHz, not 100), so MHz ratios give EPRE errors up to about 0.25 dB.
Q: What does equal power do to coverage when the bandwidths differ?
A: The narrow carrier gets a higher PSD, so higher RSRP and a bigger footprint than the wide one: 6.02 dB for LTE 5 + 20 MHz. Cell edges and reselection no longer match.
Q: What should the RU do if switching off one carrier leaves the other below the band minimum power?
A: Keep the surviving carrier on air, raise TX-out-of-order (MAJOR) and a configuration fault attributed to the carrier gain, rather than shutting the band.
Q: A 15 kHz and a 30 kHz carrier have the same EPRE. Do they have the same coverage?
A: No. The 30 kHz carrier spreads that EPRE over twice the bandwidth, so its PSD is 3 dB lower and SNR per RE is about 3 dB worse. Add 10·log10(30/15) = 3 dB to equalise.
CA2CC02 2CC conformance for Medium-Range BS — NR n78 (NRTC1/2/3, TS 38.141-1) and LTE B3 Mini-Metro: composite vs single-carrier tests, limits, gap points, IM3 placement RCT click to expand ▾
In plain English
CA2CC01 explains the idea of a composite 2CC conformance test in LTE. This card is the practical companion for two real plans: NR n78 Medium-Range (TS 38.141-1, 30 kHz SCS, 40 and 50 MHz carriers) and LTE B3 Mini-Metro Medium-Range (TS 36.141). The three things people get wrong are: using LTE clause numbers and ETC names for NR; assuming every test becomes a two-carrier test (several stay single-carrier); and copying the 1CC limits, especially the 65 ns TAE, into a CA test. It also covers where to put the carriers so the worst-case IM3 lands in your own UL band, and which sub-block gaps you need to switch on all the in-gap requirements.
Non-contiguous 2CC: the gap decides which requirements apply
Two test points, about 10 MHz and 20 MHz or more, switch on every in-gap requirement.
Level 1 — core facts
NR test configurations (TS 38.141-1 §4.7): NRTC1 contiguous, NRTC2 contiguous CA occupied bandwidth, NRTC3 non-contiguous (adds CACLR); NRTC4/5 are inter-band. Crosswalk to LTE: ETC1 ↔ NRTC1, ETC2 ↔ NRTC2, ETC3 ↔ NRTC3. Power allocation in NRTC1/2/3 is equal PSD with the sum equal to the rated total (see PSPLIT01).

RequirementNR clauseLTE clause
Occupied bandwidth6.6.26.6.1
ACLR / CACLR6.6.36.6.2
Operating band unwanted emissions6.6.46.6.3
Tx spurious6.6.56.6.4
Frequency error / EVM / TAE6.5.2 / 6.5.3 / 6.5.46.5.1 / 6.5.2 / 6.5.3
Composite vs single-carrier (TS 38.141-1 Table 4.8.3-1). Composite under 2CC: output power, ON/OFF, EVM, TAE, ACLR, OBUE, spurious, Tx-IMD, ACS, blocking, Rx spurious, Rx IMD. Stay single-carrier (per CC): total power dynamic range, reference sensitivity, dynamic range, in-channel selectivity, PRACH.

TAE in CA: 130 ns contiguous, 260 ns non-contiguous. The 65 ns value is the 1CC/MIMO limit (see NRTX01) and was still in the automation as an open item.

Intra-band CA spacing: nominal (BW1 + BW2)/2, which may be reduced to the next lower multiple of 300 kHz to pack carriers; 20 + 20 MHz → 19.8 MHz.
Level 2 — limits, combinations and test points
n78 Mini-Metro bench KPIs (2CC plan)
ItemBench targetNote
Output power per carrier24 dBm ± 1 (1CC) → 21 dBm ± 1 (2CC)shared budget, −3 dB each for equal BW
EVM (256QAM)3.5 %composite
Frequency error±185 Hz0.05 ppm at 3.65 GHz
ACLR54 dB target3GPP limit 45 dB
Transmitter OFF power / transient−85 dBm/MHz / 17 µscomposite
REFSENS−90.6 dBmsingle carrier
PRACH≥ 99 % detection, ≤ 0.1 % false alarmper CC
NR carrier combinations. NRTC1: 40 + 50 MHz (≈ 90 MHz aggregated). NRTC2: 40+40, 40+50, 50+40, 50+50, where the order says which CC sits at the lower edge. For 40+40 and 50+50 a flat −3 dB per carrier is equal PSD; for 40+50 and 50+40 it is not (≈1 dB between the carriers, see PSPLIT01).

LTE B3 Medium-Range limits. Prated,c ≤ 38 dBm per carrier. ACLR/CACLR: 45 dB or −25 dBm/MHz absolute, whichever is less stringent. Receiver tests use the wanted signal at REFSENS + 6 dB = −90.5 dBm with in-band blocking interferer −38 dBm, Rx IMD −47 dBm and narrowband blocking −44 dBm.

Sub-block gap points (B3, two 20 MHz carriers; the 75 MHz band allows gaps up to ≈35 MHz):
In-gap requirementSwitches on at
CACLR5 ≤ W_gap < 15 MHz (2.5 MHz offset); 10 < W_gap < 20 MHz (7.5 MHz offset)
Narrowband Rx IMDW_gap ≥ 5 MHz
ACLR 1st adjacent, in-band blockingW_gap ≥ 15 MHz
ACLR 2nd adjacentW_gap ≥ 20 MHz
So two gap points, about 10 MHz and 20 MHz or more, cover every threshold. Confirm the exact gap against the declared maximum non-contiguous RF bandwidth.
Level 3 — expert detail and pitfalls
IM3 placement. Two DL carriers through one PA self-mix into IM3 at 2f0 − f1 and 2f1 − f0. Each product is 2·BW(near) + BW(far) wide (20 + 20 MHz → 60 MHz). Choose the carrier placements where an IM3 product lands inside your own UL band: that is the worst case for Tx-IMD and for receiver self-desensitisation through the duplexer. If an unexpected in-band spur appears, classify it with IMD2CC01 before blaming the PA.

Pitfalls seen in real plans.
• Wrong TAE limit: the automation still used the 65 ns 1CC value for a 2CC run; the CA limits are 130/260 ns.
• Flat −3 dB for unequal bandwidths: correct for 40+40, wrong for 40+50 in a conformance run.
• LTE clause numbers in an NR report: NR ACLR is 6.6.3, not 6.6.2; frequency error 6.5.2, not 6.5.1.
• Making single-carrier tests composite: REFSENS, dynamic range, in-channel selectivity and PRACH stay per CC; running them with both carriers on changes the test.
• Declaration-dependent rows: whether the contiguous and non-contiguous configurations use identical parameters is a manufacturer declaration; if identical, several NRTC1 rows collapse to NRTC3 only.
• ETC1 vs ETC3 with only two carriers: they describe almost the same set-up; what changes is the gap and therefore the in-gap requirements.
Interview Q&A
Q: Which NR test configuration adds CACLR, and what is its LTE equivalent?
A: NRTC3 (non-contiguous spectrum), equivalent to LTE ETC3.
Q: Is reference sensitivity measured with both carriers on in a 2CC NR test?
A: No. Per Table 4.8.3-1 it stays single-carrier, as do dynamic range, in-channel selectivity, total power dynamic range and PRACH.
Q: What TAE limit applies to a contiguous 2CC n78 configuration?
A: 130 ns (260 ns non-contiguous). The 65 ns value is for MIMO/1CC transmitter diversity and is the wrong limit here.
Q: You have 75 MHz of B3 and two 20 MHz carriers. How many gap points do you need for the in-gap tests?
A: Two: about 10 MHz (CACLR and narrowband Rx IMD) and 20 MHz or more (ACLR 1st and 2nd adjacent plus in-band blocking). The maximum gap is about 35 MHz.
Q: Two 20 MHz carriers: what is the minimum intra-band CA spacing and the IM3 bandwidth?
A: Nominal 20 MHz reduced to the 300 kHz raster gives 19.8 MHz. Each IM3 product is 2·20 + 20 = 60 MHz wide.
RU tools, calibration & frequency planning
RUCLI01 RU DVT CLI (cli-manager) — RF-path commands: IQ playback/record, CW, attenuation & gains, RSSI, RFFE/PA/LNA, RF-GPIO manual TX/RX, AGC RCT click to expand ▾
In plain English
Every AAU / Mini-Metro RU runs a debug console called ru-dvt-cli (the binary is cli-manager). It is the bench engineer's steering wheel for the RF path: play a stored IQ waveform out of any antenna, record what an ADC sees, inject a pure CW tone, trim DAC/ADC attenuation and digital gains, read RSSI, flip PA/LNA enables and RF front-end (RFFE) switches, and even take the TX/RX switches away from the TDD engine and drive them by hand. Before release 2026.2 a lot of this was done by poking FPGA addresses with mw.l/md.l; the FPGA register refactor in 2026.2 moved those addresses and broke every such script. The CLI now resolves addresses from generated CSR headers, so always use the command, never a hard-coded address. This card covers the RF-path commands; the platform/OAM side of the same CLI (access, alarms, firmware, EEPROM) is a separate card, and per-RFFE test automation that drives these commands is in RFFE01 and FC20.
What cli-manager reaches
The CLI is a separate process: anything it writes can be overwritten by operations_manager (carrier reconfigure, personality re-apply) or fault_manager.
Level 1 — access, permissions and the command families
Access: on the RU shell, telnet localhost 8888; the prompt is CLI:/>. If cli-manager is not running, start it as root (as another user it crashes). help -a lists everything, help -d lists the hidden DEBUG commands, and <Tab> on an empty line lists all commands. The framework matches only the first word of a line, which is why every feature has separate set-X / get-X commands.
Permission levels: DEBUG (hidden, raw register surfaces), ROOT, USER (all users) and RFAL (RF alignment; e.g. set-antenna-power <0-40 W> needs it).
FamilyMain commandsWhat it is for
