Five finalists between 6144 and 7372.8 MS/s were deliberately left unranked: the choice depends on FPGA cost, power, DPD-rate compatibility and lab results, not on one figure of merit.
Level 3 — lessons and pitfalls
  • Fs-dependent DPD words. DPD NCO words are round(NCO/Fs_OBS × 2^48). Change Fs_OBS and forget to recompute them, and DPD observes the wrong frequency, diverges and the spectrum regrows (DPD02). The same applies to the CW generator FCW (CWGEN01).
  • Harmonics are not images. HD2/HD3 come from the DAC's analog non-linearity, so no amount of interpolation filtering removes them; only Fs choice (where they fold) and the analog filter help.
  • One tile, one Fs. Blocks in a DAC tile share the sample clock, so a dual-band variant cannot pick independent rates for two bands on the same tile.
  • Same Fc, different images. B3 at 1842.5 MHz produces different image sets on B0103 (9830.40) and on B0307 (5898.24) — image checks must be per variant, not per band (see the spectrum plots in ADC02).
  • Low sinc loss is a warning, not a comfort. When an image sits only 0.2–1 dB down the sinc (e.g. N41 1Fs−2Fc at 712 MHz), the BPF alone protects the neighbour band. Those frequencies go straight into the transmitter-spurious scan (FC19).
  • Process over intuition. Enumerate every P/Q × interpolation × mode row, give each a verdict with a reason, and keep the rejects documented — the N41 study was itself corrected later (signal-BW assumption, HD2/HD3 folding) precisely because every elimination was written down and could be re-checked.
Interview Q&A
Q: ADC Fs 2949.12 MS/s, Fc 2593 MHz: which Nyquist zone and what NCO?
A: Fs/2 = 1474.56, so NZ2. NCO = Fs − Fc = 356.12 MHz (equivalent to tuning 2593).
Q: Why does a change of DAC or OBS sample rate force a DPD config change?
A: DPD NCO words are a fraction of Fs_OBS (round(NCO/Fs_OBS × 2^48)) and the DPD rate is input × P/Q. Stale words make DPD look at the wrong frequency and diverge.
Q: Where does HD3 of a 2593 MHz carrier land at Fs = 6144 MS/s?
A: 3 × 2593 = 7779; 7779 mod 6144 = 1635, below Fs/2, so 1635 MHz.
Q: Why is "194 MHz bandwidth" the wrong input for planning n41?
A: It is the tuning range. The signal is 40 MHz; what matters is that the 40 MHz fits the usable band at every placement (BOT/MID/TOP).
Q: Bypass or IMR?
A: Same SFDR. Bypass gives the widest usable band (0–0.45 Fs); IMR halves DUC speed and power but restricts the band (HPF 0.3–0.45 Fs). Prefer NZ1 + Bypass when it fits.
RU platform health — FPGA, uSleep, reboots, crashes, serials
RUFPGA01 RU FPGA Map — XCZU67DR build variants, DFE IP blocks, rf_gpio TDD registers and the power budget RCT click to expand ▾
In plain English
Every PW AAU / Mini-Metro radio is built around one chip: a Xilinx/AMD Zynq UltraScale+ RFSoC, part XCZU67DR. It contains the ARM cores that run Linux and the M-plane, the RF data converters (DACs and ADCs that sit right at the RF/IF boundary), a set of hardened DFE (digital front end) IP blocks, and programmable fabric. The same silicon is used for every band, but each product gets its own FPGA bitstream: the band, carrier count, DPD rate and feature set are fixed when the bitstream is built. This card is a map of that chip from an RF engineer's point of view: which build goes with which radio, which IP block does CFR, DPD, PRACH and mixing, how the rf_gpio block drives the PA/LNA switches in TDD, and where the 18 W of FPGA power actually goes. For the software platform around it see RUPLAT01; for the Micro-Sleep registers that live in the same block see USLEEP01.
RFSoC datapath inside one RU
Simplified. The PS (ARM) side runs Linux, M-plane and the DPD/calibration apps; rf_gpio sits in the PL and drives the front-end switches.
Level 1 — Core facts

All variants share: XCZU67DR, O-RAN eCPRI fronthaul, BFP compression width 9, IQ recorder enabled, 4 antenna paths in the fabric. A bitstream supports exactly one variant; the variant is chosen at build time by the SystemVerilog package pw_ru_<variant>_pkg.sv.

VariantBand / RATNotable build optionsDPD sample rate
b1b3B1 + B3 FDD LTE4 CC, 2 DFE; CC2 can carry 2G245.76 MHz
b3b7B3 + B7 FDD2T2R per band, 1 DFE; AAU Sense, AGC, 2nd SFP MAC245.76 MHz
b8b20b28B8 + B20 FDD (B28 not configured)CC0 can carry 2G245.76 MHz
b41B41 TDD LTE, 15 kHz860.16 MHz
n78n78 TDD NR, 30 kHzAAU Sense, AGC, 2nd SFP MAC; RX-enable active-low983.04 MHz
n41n41 TDD NR, 30 kHz737.28 MHz
n101n101 TDD NR, 30 kHzonly build with the GPS simulator; RX-enable active-low491.52 MHz
n255n255 FDD NR, 15 kHz245.76 MHz
  • LTE variants are built with USE_DSP. DPD runs with 2 phases on b41, n78 and n41 (the high-rate builds) and 1 phase everywhere else, n101 included.
  • The DFE hard IPs and their AMD product guides: PRACH (PG391 v2.0), DUC-DDC Mixer (PG393 v2.0), Channel Filter (PG395 v1.1), PC-CFR (PG097 v8.0), DPD (PG076 v15.2), Equalizer (PG392).
  • On the RU the bitstreams are pre-staged as /etc/fpga/system-<flavour>.bit.gz (flavours b0103, b0307, b0407, b082028, b41, n101, n78, n78l). Personality detection picks the flavour at boot.
  • rf_gpio lives at base 0xAFFC0000 and owns the front-end control bits, the per-symbol TDD switching table and the uSleep registers.
Level 2 — How to check and debug

Which bitstream is loaded? Check the boot log / personality output for the detected flavour and compare it with the /etc/fpga file list. If detection returns UNKNOWN, the flavour overlay is missing, the DPD configuration files do not load, and dpd-app / operations-manager faults follow. Fix detection before suspecting the FPGA.

OffsetRegisterWhat it does
0x00 / 0x04grp0 / grp1Front-end bits for channels 1–4 / 5–8 (same layout in both): VPD/GBA, HSPDT, SPDT and DPD/VSWR SPDT controls, TX/RX SPDT disable, LNA1 enable and bypass, per-channel LNA2 bypass, PA LSD enable. Bit 31 tdd_mux_sel = the FPGA TDD engine drives the bits.
0x08SCWSafety code word. Writing 0xABCDEF01 lets the host drive the bits directly; writing 0 hands them back to the TDD engine.
0x0C–0x7Ctdd_ts[0..27]One entry per OFDM symbol of a 28-symbol pattern: switching time in 122.88 MHz ticks (low bits) + direction UL/DL/GP (high bits). 0xFFFFFFFF = no event.
0x80 / 0x84tdd_masking / agc_ctrlDefined, not used by any software consumer.
0x88–0xACusleep_ctrl, usleep_time, usleep_counter[8]Micro-Sleep — see USLEEP01.

How a TDD switching time is computed (from the TDD pattern apply path in tdd_support.c): every switching point in the configured pattern becomes one tdd_ts entry:

switching_time = frame_offset
               + tdd_t_offset                 (board constant)
               + tdd_pa_on_transition_time    (TX events: PA settling)
               - tdd_lna_on_transition_time   (RX events: LNA settling)
tdd_ts[i] = switching_time | direction_bits

All three offsets come from personality. After the pattern is written, software clears SCW so the TDD engine owns the GPIOs. Personality also stores two words per midboard column: rf-gpio-in-reset (safe state) and rf-gpio-rf-active (operating state). On a PA fault, o-ran-fm.c writes the safe word to grp0/grp1.

Bench check after an FPGA or driver upgrade: read back DL output power and gain per antenna, confirm PRACH detection, and confirm the DPD converges. These are the three places where a version mismatch shows up first (Level 3).

Level 3 — Expert detail and pitfalls
  • Driver and IP versions move together. The Linux driver version (e.g. dfeprach v1.8) and the IP version (e.g. xdfe-nr-prach-2.0) have separate numbers, but a new driver on an old bitstream writes to the wrong offsets. The Mixer v2.0 register map is a known example.
  • Mixer gain meaning flipped. AntennaCfg.Gain code 0 means −6 dB in one version and 0 dB in another. A 6 dB DL power step after an upgrade is the signature.
  • PRACH NCO. The driver computes the frequency control word from UserFreq, the SCS and the CC rate; anything you write straight into Frequency is overwritten. NcoGain codes: 0 = 0 dB, 1 = −3 dB, 2 = −6 dB, 3 = −9 dB.
  • DPD v15 (PG076 v15.x) changes in calibration configs: ODPENABLE may only be 0 or 4; DCLTXLOWPOWER / DCLRXLOWPOWER are now U32.30 fixed point; the capture-window (capwin) commands and DCLPSTEP were removed; recommended Magnitude Gain is 0. Old config files must be converted. See DPD02.
  • Stale DPD base address = reboot. In one release dpd-app wrote a DPD register address that was valid only for the previous bitstream, and the RU rebooted at once (see RBTCAUSE01).
  • RX-enable polarity is active-low on n78 and n101 and active-high on the other builds. Remember this before probing PA/LNA enable lines with a scope.
  • TX/RX SPDT disable (grp bit 5) resets to 1 (switch disabled). Until personality writes the rf-active word, the TX/RX switch path is off even if the DFE is running — check grp0/grp1 before blaming the RF chain.

Where the power goes — b3b7 2T2R as built:

BlockPowerNotes
RF data converters7.38 WADC 4.52 W, DAC 2.86 W — the largest single item
DFE hard blocks2.56 WFFT 0.89, CFR 0.54, FIR 0.39, NLF 0.26 W …
DPD IP≈1.5 W
DL chains (4)≈1.09 W
PRACH chain≈0.94 W
25G MAC + GTY0.76 W
Total (Vivado)18.2 W≈19.5 W with a realistic PS model

For comparison, the n78 4T4R build is about 19.1 W and b1b3 4T4R about 23.8 W. Disabling channels in software on a 4-antenna bitstream removes only a little of this: most fabric power is fixed by what is built in. That is why Micro-Sleep targets the PAs, not the FPGA (USLEEP01).

Sizing example (small-cell study). A 2T2R B39 TDD 10 MHz build with 1 CFR + 1 DPD pair was estimated at 10.4 W typical and 13.4 W at the worst corner (Tj 85 °C, max process), plus 10–15% for regulators. Fronthaul for 52 PRB × 14 symbols × 2 antennas is about 0.33 Gb/s with 9-bit BFP and 0.56 Gb/s with 16-bit IQ per direction — easily carried by PCIe Gen2 x1 or 10G, with about 46 µs UL / 17 µs DL transport latency against a < 100 µs budget.

Interview Q&A
Q: Why does each RU product have its own FPGA bitstream if the chip is the same?
A: The band plan, CC count, DFE count, DPD sample rate and options such as AAU Sense or the GPS simulator are fixed at build time through the variant package. One bitstream = one variant.
Q: After an FPGA/driver upgrade the DL power is 6 dB off. Where do you look?
A: Mixer AntennaCfg.Gain: its code meaning changed between versions (0 = −6 dB vs 0 = 0 dB). Also confirm driver and IP versions match.
Q: What does writing 0xABCDEF01 to rf_gpio SCW do?
A: It lets the host drive the front-end bits directly instead of the TDD engine. Write 0 to give control back; software does this after programming the TDD pattern.
Q: How is a TDD switching instant derived?
A: frame_offset + tdd_t_offset, plus the PA-on transition time for TX events, minus the LNA-on transition time for RX events, in 122.88 MHz ticks, written with direction bits into tdd_ts[i].
Q: What dominates FPGA power and what does that mean for energy saving?
A: The RF data converters (about 7.4 of 18.2 W on b3b7). Switching channels off in software saves little; real savings come from the PAs (Micro-Sleep) or a smaller build.
USLEEP06 Micro-Sleep operating procedure (REL_2026.3) — enable per band, verify three layers per carrier, disable, persistence, DVT CLI commands & troubleshooting RCT click to expand ▾
In plain English
USLEEP01 explains how Micro-Sleep works inside the radio; USLEEP02–05 show how to measure the saving. This card is the operator procedure for release REL_2026.3: how to switch uSleep on for one band, prove it is really engaging on every carrier, switch it off again cleanly, and why a change you made by hand disappears after a reboot. Think of it as three layers that must all agree: the YANG request (tx-feature-enable), the software that turns that request into register values (enable, pa_en), and the hardware counters that show PAs actually sleeping on blank symbols.
Three layers to verify
Request → register state → hardware evidence. A pass on one layer alone proves nothing.
Level 1 — what is supported and what the knobs are
Micro-Sleep is supported only on the Metro 4/5-band AAU flavours. Per carrier, each array column owns two pa_en bits and two counters; columns are numbered band by band in band-capabilities order, A0A1 = column 0, A2A3 = column 1, and CC0/CC1 of a band share the same column.
Flavourusleep-supportedpa_en bit map (column n owns bits 2n, 2n+1)
Metro b082028 (B8 + B28)trueB8 → bits 0–3, B28 → bits 4–7. B28 is listed as band-number 9928 (carriers TxArrayCarrierB9928C00A0A1 / A2A3)
Metro b0103 (B1 + B3)trueB1 → bits 0–3, B3 → bits 4–7
Metro b41trueB41 → bits 0–3; bits 4–7 unused
Mini Metro, B1B3, n41, MM, USGfalseevery band advertises tx-feature-support = 0, so an enable is rejected
Personality keyShipped valueMeaning / rule
usleep-supportedtrue on the three Metro flavours (GRDEV-10085)Hardware gate; if false the timing is never programmed at boot
usleep-enablefalse — leave it falseAt boot pa_en = 0x00, so true would do nothing, and the first carrier change recomputes it anyway
usleep-tx-en-advance3441 ticks (~28 µs)How early the PA is woken before a non-blank symbol
usleep-tx-dis-delay123 ticks (~1 µs)How long after the last non-blank sample the PA is gated
limitadvance + delaymust be < 4096 ticks at 30 kHz SCS or < 8192 ticks at 15 kHz SCS (ticks of 122.88 MHz)
usleep-cc-modecc0-and-cc1Both carriers on the band must be blank before the shared PA sleeps
usleep-pa-eligible255Ceiling ANDed with the derived pa_en; can only remove PAs
Control is per band, through one leaf in a PW augment of the O-RAN user-plane model: tx-feature-enable (namespace urn:pw:feat:1.0) on each tx-array-carriers entry. Its default is 0. The RU reports the result in tx-feature-state and sends a tx-feature-state-change notification.
Level 2 — enable, verify, disable (REL_2026.3 procedure)

Step 0 — pre-checks. Confirm the flavour, the personality keys, the advertised capability and the timing the software actually programmed at boot:

tr ' ' '
' </proc/cmdline | grep -E 'ru.model|ru.flavor'
grep usleep- /etc/configs/personalities/<model>-pw.json
sysrepocfg -X -d operational   -x /o-ran-module-cap:module-capability/band-capabilities   # tx-feature-support per band
grep -a usleep_init /run/media/mmcblk0p4/fhgw.log
#  usleep_init: tx_en_advance=3441 tx_dis_delay=123 cc_mode=2 enable=0
#  register usleep_time should read 0x007B0D71  (0x007B = 123, 0x0D71 = 3441)

Step 1 — enable (production path is the DU/SMO over NETCONF). One edit-config sets the leaf on every active TX array-carrier of the band:

<user-plane-configuration xmlns="urn:o-ran:uplane-conf:1.0">
  <tx-array-carriers>
    <name>TxArrayCarrierB08C00A0A1</name>
    <tx-feature-enable xmlns="urn:pw:feat:1.0">1</tx-feature-enable>
  </tx-array-carriers>
  <tx-array-carriers>
    <name>TxArrayCarrierB08C00A2A3</name>
    <tx-feature-enable xmlns="urn:pw:feat:1.0">1</tx-feature-enable>
  </tx-array-carriers>
</user-plane-configuration>

# lab, no DU: same validation and callbacks as a NETCONF edit
sudo sysrepocfg -E /tmp/usleep_on.xml -d running -f xml
  • No mixed band (SRS-7232-AAU-140): if the result would leave one band with some carriers on and some off, the edit is rejected with aau-feature-band-mismatch. Inactive carriers are not compared. Different bands are independent.
  • Only advertised bits (AAU-130): anything not in tx-feature-support is rejected with aau-feature-unsupported. Writing 0 is always accepted.
  • Rejections raise no alarm — the edit is refused before any hardware write, so look at the NETCONF reply.
  • B8 CC0 on both columns gives pa_en = 0x0F; all four carriers of b082028 give 0xFF.

Step 2 — verify all three layers. (a) tx-feature-state = 1 on each carrier in the operational datastore, plus a tx-feature-state-change notification. (b) The log lines are in /run/media/mmcblk0p4/fhgw.log, not in journalctl:

grep -a -E 'usleep_apply_state|PL micro-sleep|tx-feature-state change' /run/media/mmcblk0p4/fhgw.log | tail
usleep_apply_state: enable=1 pa_en=0x0f
PL micro-sleep: aggregate active-carrier mask 0x0f, eligible=0xff, programmed pa_en=0x0f, enable=1

(c) In the DVT CLI, run get-usleep-ctrl, then get-usleep-counters twice a few seconds apart. Each carrier must show its own two pa_en bits set and its own two counters rising.

Counter behaviourMeaning
Rising on the enabled PAsuSleep is engaging
≈ +14,000/s (15 kHz) or ≈ +28,000/s (30 kHz)Every symbol is blank: no DL traffic reaches the RU. It works, but you are not testing under load
Frozen on a PA outside pa_enExpected: that PA is held awake; the counter is frozen, not cleared
0 under full DU trafficCan be correct: there are no blank symbols to sleep in

Step 3 — disable. Set tx-feature-enable = 0 (or delete the leaf; its default is 0) on the same carriers. Expect enable=0 pa_en=0x00. Counters keep their last value; clear them with usleep-clear-counters 255. Then prove that only uSleep changed: the same number of ACTIVE carriers, TX carriers still READY, GPIO GRP0/GRP1 PA-enable words unchanged, no new entry in /o-ran-fm:active-alarm-list. Deactivating every carrier also switches uSleep off.

Automated check. A read-only script, usleep_check.py, reads sysrepo, the registers (through /etc/fpga/fpga-lib.sh) and the counters, and prints one verdict per carrier: PASS, OFF (as requested), INACTIVE, or FAIL with the reason (enable=0, pa_en bits missing, tx-feature-state=0, counters not moving, or a 2CC band on a build without GRDEV-10354). Exit code 0/1 makes it usable in a pipeline (see USLEEP05).

Level 3 — CLI reference, persistence and pitfalls

Lab forcing through the DVT CLI is for bring-up only and does not stick: any tx-array-carrier change makes operations-manager recompute enable and pa_en from YANG. Since Aug 2026 the four tx-* timing commands take a band argument; older scripts fail argument validation. With intra-band 2CC on older builds, software force-disables uSleep and logs PL micro-sleep force-disabled.

DVT CLI commandWhat it does
get-usleep-ctrlenable, cc_mode and pa_en in one line, e.g. enable=1, cc_mode=0, pa_en=0xFF
set-usleep-ctrl 0|1Global enable bit. On its own it does nothing while pa_en = 0x00
get/set-usleep-cc-mode 0|1|2Which carrier decides a symbol is empty: 0 = cc0 master, 1 = cc1 master, 2 = both carriers must be blank
set-usleep-pa-en <0-255>Bitmap, bit n = PA n takes part; a PA with its bit clear stays on
get/set-usleep-tx-en-advance <band 0-1> [0-65535]PA wake-up advance, 122.88 MHz ticks (1 µs ≈ 123 ticks)
get/set-usleep-tx-dis-delay <band 0-1> [ticks]0–288 at 30 kHz SCS, 0–576 at 15 kHz; capped at the PL FIFO read point and validated against the advance
get-usleep-countersBlank-symbol (sleep) count per PA — the hardware proof
usleep-clear-counters <bitmap>Clears the selected counters (255 = all)
# force on (lab only) - pa_en first, otherwise enable=1 changes nothing
set-usleep-pa-en 0xFF
set-usleep-ctrl 1
# unsupported flavour: FPGA keeps reset values (advance 615, cc_mode 0)
# set the delay first, because the advance is checked against the current delay
set-usleep-tx-dis-delay <band> 123
set-usleep-tx-en-advance <band> 3441
set-usleep-cc-mode 2
EventEffect on a uSleep enable
RU reboot after a local sysrepocfg editLost — the edit lived in running; startup still holds the default 0
DU re-pushes the carrier config without the leafReverts to 0
Any carrier activate/deactivateenable and pa_en recomputed; CLI forcing overwritten
Lasting enableOnly from the DU / SMO configuration

Troubleshooting

  • A 2CC band stays awake: builds before GRDEV-10354 (merged 2026-10-05) cannot sleep a 2CC band; with the fix it needs cc_mode=2.
  • "User callback failed" when activating a second carrier is not uSleep: the combined carrier gain (23.01 dB in the recorded case) exceeded the tx-array max-gain of 20 dB. Lower the per-carrier gain.
  • tx-en-advance rejected: advance + delay is over the 4096 / 8192 tick limit.
  • One PA of a pair never counts after a reboot (seen once on b0103 PA[7]) is not root-caused: record build, model and PA number and report it rather than working around it.
  • Counters at +14k/+28k per second on every PA mean your "traffic" test has no DL traffic — fix the DU/test signal before reading power (USLEEP04).

Validation record. b082028, b0103 and b41 all passed enable, band-mismatch rejection and disable on 2026.3.0-100 with 1CC. Not yet covered: 2CC with GRDEV-10354, and the energy saving under real traffic (USLEEP02/05 cover the power side).

Interview Q&A
Q: How do you switch uSleep on for one band in production?
A: One NETCONF edit-config setting tx-feature-enable = 1 (namespace urn:pw:feat:1.0) on every active tx-array-carrier of that band. Partial bands are rejected with aau-feature-band-mismatch.
Q: tx-feature-state is 1. Is uSleep working?
A: Not proven. Also check the fhgw.log apply line (enable=1, expected pa_en) and that each carrier's own two counters rise between two get-usleep-counters reads.
Q: Counters rise by about 28,000 per second on every PA. Good or bad?
A: uSleep engages, but every 30 kHz symbol is blank — there is no DL traffic, so you are not testing under load.
Q: You enabled uSleep with set-usleep-ctrl 1 and nothing happened. Why?
A: pa_en is 0x00 after boot, so no PA takes part. Set set-usleep-pa-en first. And any carrier change will overwrite the forced values anyway.
Q: Why did the enable disappear after a reboot?
A: It was a local edit in running; startup still holds 0, and a DU re-push without the leaf also reverts it. A lasting enable must come from the DU/SMO.
RBTEV01 Reboot Event Subsystem (GRDEV-9680) — one cause per reboot, O-RAN restart-cause mapping, RESET_REASON bits and the JSONL history RCT click to expand ▾
In plain English
When a radio reboots in the field, the SMO asks one question: why? The RU answers through the O-RAN restart-cause leaf. On older builds that answer was almost always POWER-ON, because only ruReset() callers wrote a reason file and operations_manager emptied it at every start, often before anyone read it. Script reboots, kernel panics and watchdog resets were never recorded. The Reboot Event Subsystem (GRDEV-9680, which replaces the GRDEV-7271 design described in RBTCAUSE01) fixes this: every reboot path writes exactly one record before it reboots, and a boot-time service fills in the cause for reboots that had no chance to write anything (panic, watchdog, power loss) from hardware evidence. Every boot also appends one line to a JSONL history, so a 100-reboot stability run becomes a table of causes instead of a pile of logs. The low-level crash evidence it relies on (the PGGS1 boot stage and last_shutdown) is covered in CRASH01.
One cause per reboot: recorded or derived
Paths and service names as on REL_2026.x builds.
Level 1 — Core facts
  • Entry points. RU_RESET_ORDERLY() reboots through systemctl reboot; RU_RESET_IMMEDIATE() flushes logs then calls reboot(2). Both first write the record: cause, requester and the file:line:function of the caller. Shell scripts use save-reboot-event <cause> ["info"] with options --unless-pending, --requester=, --origin=.
  • Requesters: smo, local-operator (anyone on a console or ssh login, from /proc/self/loginuid, which survives sudo — SSH_CONNECTION was rejected because sudo clears it), ru-software, systemd, unrequested (cause derived at boot), unknown.
  • Recorded causes: supervision-watchdog, mplane-triggered-restart (NETCONF reset), software-upgrade, system-watchdog (wd_manager), restart, component-update (timing-chip frequency plan, start_transmission), diagnostic-triggered-restart (DVT CLI / I2C check), software-failure (network fail-fast). Derived only: kernel-panic and system-unresponsive.
Internal causeO-RAN restart-cause
power-onPOWER-ON
supervision-watchdogSUPERVISION-WATCHDOG
software-failure, kernel-panicSOFTWARE-FAILURE
system-watchdog, system-unresponsiveOTHER-WATCHDOG-TIMER
mplane-triggered-restart, software-upgrade, restartMPLANE-TRIGGERED-RESTART only if requester = smo; otherwise UNKNOWN
(never reported)DEEP-HIBERNATE-RESTART

The mapping switch has no default case on purpose: a new cause will not compile until someone maps it.

Level 2 — How to read and test it

Read the result on the RU and from the SMO side:

show-reboot-event              # the record for this boot
show-reboot-event --history    # one line per boot from reboot-event-history.jsonl
ru-dvt-cli get-reboot-event    # same, from the DVT CLI
save-reboot-event --clear      # delete the record; next boot derives the cause itself
# SMO / NETCONF: o-ran-operations restart-cause, plus the PW restart-info augment
#   (pw-operations.yang) with the reboot-chain list

Bench pass criteria — a ready-made test plan for a new build:

Actionrestart-causeInternal cause / last_shutdown
NETCONF reset RPCMPLANE-TRIGGERED-RESTARTmplane-triggered-restart, requester smo
reboot over sshUNKNOWNrestart, requester local-operator; orderly
echo c > /proc/sysrq-triggerSOFTWARE-FAILUREkernel-panic; panic
FPD or LPD watchdog expiryOTHER-WATCHDOG-TIMERsystem-unresponsive; hard-reset
sysrq-b (emergency reboot)UNKNOWNemergency
Power cyclePOWER-ONpower-on; power-loss
Two reboots before in-servicefirst cause keptreboot-chain has three entries

Main vs secondary events. A reboot requested before the /run/ru-in-service marker exists becomes a secondary event: restart-cause keeps reporting the original (main) cause, and the full chain is in reboot-chain. This stops a boot-time retry from hiding the reboot that actually matters.

Level 3 — Expert detail and pitfalls

How settle-boot-cause decides (oneshot, once per boot): if a pending record exists, use its cause. Otherwise, in order:

  • last_shutdown = panic → kernel-panic
  • RESET_REASON = 0x00, or bit 0x04 set → system-unresponsive (watchdog)
  • RESET_REASON exactly 0x01 → power-on
  • anything else → unknown

It then clears the RESET_REASON bits it read and stores them in the record.

CRL_APB.RESET_REASON (0xFF5E0220) bitMeaning
0x01 external_porPower-on, or a PCB watchdog pulling PS_POR_B. Power-on resets the register to exactly 0x01
0x04 pmu_sys_resetLPD system watchdog (SWDT) expiry
0x08 PS-only resetCleared by the FSBL, so rarely seen
0x20 softreboot, sysrq-b, U-Boot reset
0x00Both a kernel panic and an FPD SWDT reset read 0 — the register cannot separate them; the PGGS1 boot stage (CRASH01) can
  • Watchdogs. The LPD SWDT is fed only by network-watchdog.service: /dev/watchdog1, 60 s timeout, a write every 30 s; expiry shows as RESET_REASON 0x04. The CSU watchdog trips if the PMU firmware stalls for 90 ms (500 ms during a PL load). The board-level external watchdog is described in RBTCAUSE01.
  • Files on p4. The record is O-RAN/log/reboot-event, a JSON object whose only mandatory key is version. History: reboot-event-history.jsonl, about 400 B per boot, rotated at 64 KiB into one .1 file. Readers return OK, MISSING, TRUNCATED, FOREIGN, NEWER or CORRUPT, so a half-written file after a power cut is handled, not trusted.
  • Timestamps. restart-datetime is written only when ntp_adjtime() reports a synchronised clock; uptime is always written. A missing datetime is normal on a bench without PTP/NTP.
  • Open item — endless reboot loop. U-Boot counts trial boots (bootlimit 4) only while upgrade_available=1. A slot that was already accepted and then fails at every start-up reboot-loops forever and Recovery never runs. A proposed reboot-loop alarm would read this history.
  • Typical symptom on old builds. A reboot-soak reports POWER-ON for nearly every cycle even though the unit was never power-cycled. With GRDEV-9680 the history file shows the real mix (script restarts, watchdog, panic) with the call site of each request.
Interview Q&A
Q: Why did older RU builds report POWER-ON after almost every reboot?
A: Only ruReset() callers wrote the reason, and operations_manager emptied it at every start. Script reboots, panics and watchdog resets left nothing, so the default POWER-ON was reported.
Q: A kernel panic and an FPD watchdog reset both give RESET_REASON 0x00. How are they told apart?
A: By the PGGS1 boot stage, written by the crash-record kmsg dumper: a panic sets last_shutdown = panic, a watchdog leaves RUNNING set and reads as hard-reset.
Q: A field engineer reboots the RU over ssh. What does the SMO see?
A: UNKNOWN. The cause is restart with requester local-operator; only an smo requester maps restart-type causes to MPLANE-TRIGGERED-RESTART.
Q: What is a secondary reboot event?
A: A reboot requested before the in-service marker. restart-cause keeps the original main cause; the full sequence is in the reboot-chain list.
Q: Why is local-operator taken from loginuid and not SSH_CONNECTION?
A: loginuid survives sudo; sudo clears SSH_CONNECTION, so a sudo reboot would otherwise look like it came from the software.
CRASH01 Crash Record in reserved RAM (GRDEV-10558) — pstore/ramoops, PGGS1 boot stages, last_shutdown and limits on a stalled reboot RCT click to expand ▾
In plain English
To save eMMC wear, the RU keeps its logs in RAM at runtime (GRDEV-10352). The price: when the kernel panics or a watchdog resets the SoC, everything that explained the crash vanished with the RAM contents. On top of that, kernel.panic was 0, so a panic just froze the CPUs and the FPD watchdog reset the unit about 32 s later (23–45 s seen) — which then looked like an ordinary watchdog reset. The Crash Record (GRDEV-10558) reserves a small piece of DDR that Linux never maps and uses the standard Linux pstore/ramoops mechanism to keep the panic dump, the kernel console and the newest application log there. DDR keeps its contents across a warm reset, so the next boot can read and archive them. A persistent PMU register (PGGS1) records the boot stage, so the next boot also knows how the previous one ended. RBTEV01 turns that answer into the O-RAN restart-cause.
Where the crash evidence lives
Sizes and addresses from the GRDEV-10558 design.
Level 1 — Core facts
Boot stage (PGGS1 bits 3-0)last_shutdown at next bootMeaning
1 READING_REGIONread-faultThe previous boot crashed while reading the crash region itself
2 RUNNING (still set)hard-resetWatchdog reset or hang — nothing got to write a later stage
3 ORDERLY_SHUTDOWNorderlyPID 1 performed the reboot
4 FORCED_SHUTDOWNforcedreboot(2) called from another task
5 KERNEL_PANICpanicKernel panic
6 EMERGENCY_RESTARTemergencysysrq-b
tag missing / stage 0power-lossPGGS1 was cleared by a power-on
  • Read it from /sys/bus/platform/drivers/crash-record/last_shutdown.
  • Boot-slot field: 1/2 = application slots, 3 = Recovery, 4 = Recovery copy.
  • The stage is written by crash_record_dump(), a kmsg dumper registered with max_reason=KMSG_DUMP_SHUTDOWN. It updates PGGS1 through an SMC call to the PMU firmware and allocates nothing on the panic path. An oops writes no stage, because it does not end the boot.
  • Kernel config: CONFIG_PSTORE=y, PSTORE_RAM, PSTORE_CONSOLE, PSTORE_PMSG, deflate compression. systemd-pstore.service is masked so nothing is copied to the root partition.
  • rsyslog sends every fhgw.log line to /dev/pmsg0 through ompipe. omfile would create an ever-growing file in RAM instead.
Level 2 — How to use and test it

After an unexpected reboot, look here first:

cat /sys/bus/platform/drivers/crash-record/last_shutdown   # panic, hard-reset, orderly ...
show-reboot-event                                          # cause as reported (RBTEV01)
ls <p4>/logs/boot-<N>/pstore/
#   dmesg-ramoops-*     panic / oops dump
#   console-ramoops-0   kernel console of the crashed boot
#   pmsg-ramoops-0      tail of fhgw.log (~7.5 min)
#   found.txt           why the archive was taken

At boot, ru-log-store copies the records into p4/logs/boot-<N>/pstore/ with a found.txt, then deletes them from pstore. Retention keeps at most 20 archives and 512 MiB in total.

Bench testExpected result
Power cutRegion zeroed at boot, no EDAC or AXI error; last_shutdown = power-loss
echo c > /proc/sysrq-triggerOne boot-<N> archive with the dump; last_shutdown = panic
kill -STOP the hw-watchdog daemon (FPD SWDT)Archive with console and pmsg; hard-reset
kill -STOP network-watchdog (LPD SWDT)Archive with console and pmsg; hard-reset
Normal runningeMMC write counters do not change — the feature itself must not write to flash

Bench result on the design: the region survived a U-Boot reset, a normal reboot, FPD and LPD SWDT resets and a panic.

Level 3 — Expert detail and pitfalls
  • Zero with DC ZVA, never memset. After a power-on a DDR line has no valid ECC check bits. A partial 16-byte stp store makes the controller read the rest of the line, which raised an AXI error on a lab unit. The probe checks DCZID_EL0 (bit 4, DZP) and refuses to load if DC ZVA is prohibited. Zeroing the region is 8192 cache lines and takes under 1 ms.
  • Read guard. Before reading the region, the probe writes READING_REGION to PGGS1, sets panic_timeout to 10 s and registers a die notifier that turns an oops into a panic. A corrupt region therefore costs at most one boot, and the next boot reports read-fault instead of looping.
  • Power cut vs watchdog. Cuts of about 3–5 s cleared PGGS1 and set RESET_REASON to 0x01 (power-loss). A very short cut may keep PGGS1 and read as hard-reset, the same as a watchdog. Using the power-fail GPIO to tell them apart is proposed, not tested.
  • Proposed: CONFIG_PANIC_TIMEOUT=10, so a panic reboots by software in 10 s instead of waiting about 32 s for the watchdog.

Limits on a stalled reboot, from least to most disruptive — useful when a reboot "hangs" on the bench:

StageIf it stallslast_shutdown
RU_RESET_ORDERLY grace periodreboot(2) is called directlyforced
PID 1 job timeout on reboot.target / poweroff.targetShortened from the stock 30 minorderly
sysrq timersync, remount read-only, rebootemergency
Proposed: RebootWatchdogSec=2min + watchdog.stop_on_reboot=0FPD SWDT ends a hang inside the kernelhard-reset

The Cadence watchdog driver accepts at most 516 s, which is why the systemd default of 10 min could not be used.

Interview Q&A
Q: How can logs survive a kernel panic on a unit that does not write eMMC at runtime?
A: pstore/ramoops in a reserved DDR region that Linux never maps; DDR keeps its contents across a warm reset, and the next boot archives the records to p4.
Q: How does the next boot know whether the last one ended in a panic, a watchdog reset or a power cut?
A: From the PGGS1 boot stage: panic writes stage 5, a watchdog leaves RUNNING set (hard-reset), and a power-on clears the register (power-loss).
Q: Why must the region be zeroed with DC ZVA after a power-on?
A: Fresh DDR has no valid ECC; a partial store forces a read-modify-write of an ECC-invalid line and raises an AXI error. DC ZVA writes full lines.
Q: Why does rsyslog use ompipe to /dev/pmsg0?
A: pmsg is the pstore zone for user-space logs; omfile would grow a file in RAM and the content would not survive a warm reset.
Q: Why did a panic used to look like a watchdog reset?
A: kernel.panic was 0, so the CPUs just halted and the FPD watchdog reset the unit about 32 s later; RESET_REASON reads 0x00 for both.
SERNO01 RU Serial Number & EEPROM Map — 15+1 format, partitions, read-out and Alarm-16 recovery RCT click to expand ▾
In plain English
The serial number is how the DU, the SMO and the dashboards tell one radio from another. On PW RUs and FHGWs it lives in a small I2C EEPROM next to the MAC addresses, the model name and the RF calibration words. It looks simple, but it has caught many people out: the EEPROM stores 15 characters, the RU reports 16 (it appends the last character of the model name), and a newer firmware check rejects anything that is not exactly 15. Units programmed by hand with a longer serial therefore raise Alarm/Fault 16 after a firmware update and need a short recovery. This card explains the format, where it sits in the EEPROM map, how to read it safely, and how to recover. For burning the calibration partition of the same EEPROM see CAL01.
15 + 1: how the serial is built
Field widths per the shipped eeprom.json. The width is configuration, not a constant.
Level 1 — Core facts
  • Format. 4+2+1+4+4 = prefix, HW revision, manufacturer code, MMYY date, sequence. The prefix selects the product and its capabilities file; the date code must parse as MMYY and must not be in the future.
  • Character rules. Production ATE accepts decimal digits only, exactly 15. Firmware is wider: hex characters (0-9, a-f, A-F) with at least one decimal digit, no internal spaces. Leading/trailing whitespace (including the CR of a CRLF line) is trimmed before counting.
  • Length is exactly 15 (GRDEV-9427): shorter is refused as well as longer. A short stored serial now gives an empty read and Fault 16, instead of composing a nonsense identity such as a 3-character serial the DU cannot bind. Letters such as P or W are rejected because they are not hex.
EEPROM partitionLocation / sizeContents
P1 identity2 KB at 0x0000Serial at offset 29; three MAC addresses at 128/136/144, each with CRC16; model name at 162
P2 RF calibration3 KB at 0x0800DSA per channel (0–31.5 dB), CLGC loop gain (0–74.0), calibration status at 0x840 (see CAL01)
P0at 0x1400Credential hash and last reset reason
P3at 5225DVT FRU serials

Device: I2C bus 1, address 0x54, exposed as /sys/bus/i2c/devices/i2c-1/1-0054/eeprom. The layout comes from /etc/configs/eeprom.json; the same layout applies to RU and FHGW.

Level 2 — How to read, check and recover

Read it (read-only, safe on any unit):

E=/sys/bus/i2c/devices/i2c-1/1-0054/eeprom
xxd -s 29 -l 16 $E          # stored serial (15 chars + terminator)
hexdump -C $E | head -40    # raw identity partition
cat /etc/configs/eeprom.json   # field offsets and serial-number-max-digit
# what the network sees: ietf-hardware serial-num in the operational datastore (16 chars)

Recover from Alarm 16 after a firmware update (unit programmed earlier with more than 15 characters):

  • Save a copy of /run/media/mmcblk0p4/O-RAN/eeprom_data (the eMMC backup of the EEPROM fields), then delete it so the stale long value is not restored.
  • Run flash_eeprom and set the serial again using only the first 15 characters (it must be all hex with at least one digit; an alphanumeric prefix starting with letters cannot be kept). Re-set the board revision in the same session.
  • Reboot; Alarm 16 must be gone.
  • On the BBU, undeploy and delete the vNode (or CU/DU for 5G) and create it again: the same RU MAC now reports a different serial.

Validator rule for test scripts: never hard-code 15 or 16. Read serial-number-max-digit from the installed /etc/configs/eeprom.json. Ignore the copy under support_files/ in the source tree: it is a stale older layout (13 characters at a different offset and bus).

Level 3 — Expert detail and pitfalls
AnomalyTicketWhat you see
17-character serial (suffix appended to an already-composed 16)CLD-27585, fixed in 2026.3.0Same RU appears twice in SMO / dashboards: the KPI/board-info path and M-plane serial-num differ in the last digit
Alphanumeric serial that changes across a FW upgradeGRDEV-9515Fails the 15-char and hex checks; needs the recovery above
Recovery image does not append a serialGRDEV-9265Alarm 5068 never clears while running the recovery image
Stray space in the stored serialGRDEV-6849Fault 15 "Unit Out of Order"
  • Layout bugs in the identity partition: the NUL terminator of the product-variant field overwrites the first byte of the model name, and the QPAM-front NUL overwrites the QPAM-rear field. Do not trust those two fields from a raw dump without checking the neighbours.
  • The appended suffix is not validated — it is whatever the model name ends with (today always a digit). A model-name change changes the reported serial.
  • The configured width is capped by the code at 15 (SERIAL_NUMBER_MAX_FIELD_LEN), so an eeprom.json that declares more cannot overflow the 17-byte buffer.
  • The same 16-character string goes to M-plane serial-num and to the DHCP vendor identity; a unit test asserts they match. If dashboards and SMO disagree, suspect a path that builds its own serial.
  • Changing the serial is an identity change for the whole network: DU binding, SMO inventory and KPI history all key on it. Treat it like a hardware swap.
Interview Q&A
Q: The EEPROM holds 15 characters but the SMO shows 16. Why?
A: At read-out the RU appends the last character of the model name (FHGW leg index or HW-revision digit, GRDEV-9265). 15 + 1 = 16 is by design.
Q: After a firmware update an older unit raises Alarm 16. What happened and how do you fix it?
A: It was programmed with more than 15 characters and the new check enforces exactly 15. Back up and delete eeprom_data, re-flash the first 15 characters, reboot, then re-create the vNode/CU/DU on the BBU.
Q: Why can a serial starting with PW not be programmed?
A: The firmware accepts only hex characters (plus at least one decimal digit); P and W are not hex.
Q: How would you write a serial-number check in an automation suite?
A: Read the field width from the installed eeprom.json, check hex + at least one digit + no spaces, and compare EEPROM, M-plane serial-num and DHCP identity — not a hard-coded 15/16.
Q: The same RU shows up twice in the SMO. What is a likely cause?
A: Two paths composing the serial differently (the 17-character bug CLD-27585), so one RU is keyed two ways. Fixed in 2026.3.0.
Addition — the three sources of fault 16 on a multi-board AAU, companion alarms and the backup-file format
Fault 16 "Unit unidentified" has three different sources that share one fault id on a multi-board AAU. Fixing one does not clear the others, so identify the source first.
SourceLog signatureCause
FHGW"eeprom data not match"board revision / serial differs from the eMMC backup (eeprom_data)
MB0 / MB1 (midboard)"Serial number is Zero"midboard serial all zeros
RFFE0 / RFFE1"Failed to open …json"RFFE EEPROM JSON file missing
  • Companion alarms: 15 Unit out of order (RU_INIT_STARTUP), 25 Reset requested, and 18 Synchronization error (FREERUN). 18 is S-plane and independent of M-plane identity — do not expect it to clear with fault 16.
  • Healthy backup content = board revision + 15-character base serial, e.g. "V2P1" + 15 digits = 19 characters. If the V2P1 prefix is missing, set the board revision with flash_eeprom option 3 and the serial with option 1 (15-character base only — the 16th character comes from the model name on every read), then reboot.
  • mb-get-hw-revision reports the midboard revision, not the board revision — do not mix them up (AAUUPG01).
  • On some bench builds fault 16 on every boot is a known, harmless issue (NBXG01) — check the release notes before chasing it.
# which source raised it?
sysrepocfg -X -x /o-ran-fm:active-alarm-list -d operational | grep -B2 -A8 'fault-id>16'
grep -E 'unidentif|eeprom data not match|Serial number is Zero|Failed to open.*json' \
  /run/media/mmcblk0p4/fhgw.log | tail
# confirm the fix on the BBU: the RU is listed with its serial
orncrrh_dbg
Phase 2 — uSleep campaigns, E-Tilt, test strategy & IQ capture
USLEEP07 uSleep 5-band E2E campaigns with UEs — idle/load/24 h call model, re-runs, third-party RRU baseline and the B1 MCS side-effect RCT click to expand ▾
In plain English
USLEEP01 explains how uSleep blanks the PA on empty OFDM symbols, USLEEP02 and USLEEP04 explain how to measure it, and USLEEP05 gives the RCT-lab numbers with a fixed test signal and no UEs. This card is the end-to-end answer with real handsets: a 5-band AAU (three radios: B1+B3, B8+B28, B41 TDD) carrying 10 UEs, measured over three campaigns on 2026.3.0 and two re-runs, including a 48-hour realistic call model and a comparison against a third-party single-band RRU.

Short version: at idle uSleep saves about 220-240 W per AAU (about 30%), at light load about 100 W, at a steady 50% load nothing, and over a realistic 24 h traffic day about 57 W (4.7%), roughly 1.4 kWh per unit per day, with no KPI impact on the standard counters. But a closer look at link adaptation found a side-effect: on B1, uSleep ON pushes the MCS distribution several indices lower, so the cell needs more PRBs for the same throughput. A power saving you only see on the meter can hide a cost you only see in the scheduler.
What uSleep is worth on a real 5-band AAU
Bars to scale (2 px per W). Unit noise at a given load is up to about 40 W, so loaded differences below that are reported, not claimed.
Level 1 — the results
Setup. Three radios, five 4T4R cells (B1, B3, B28 and B41 at 20 MHz, B8 at 10 MHz; B41 TDD), 2 UEs per cell, TCP iperf3 with a per-cell feedback loop holding each cell at its PRB target. Power = the RU's own per-band PM power objects (O-RAN-B1/B2 per radio), 15-min averages on 2026.3.0 and 5-min on 2026.3.1. Campaign A was a single 0-90% sweep, campaign B five repeated loops of 0/30/50% ON then OFF, campaign C 24 h ON then 24 h OFF under a continuous bidirectional call model with UEs handing over between mid-band and low-band.
ScenarioLoad (DL PRB)OFFONSavingNotes
Idle (campaign B, 5 loops)~0%757 W540 W217 W (28.7%)load-matched, high confidence
Idle re-run, 13 Oct~0%766 W526 W240 W (31%)B28 raised to 46 dBm
Idle re-run, 28 Oct (2026.3.1, 5-min PM)~0%778 W544 W234 W (30.1%)6 x 5-min bins per state, about ±3 W
Light load (campaign B)~30%1,049 W949 W99 W (9.5%)about 87 ± 14 W at the same PRB
Steady 50% (campaign B)~50%1,229 W1,228 W0 WPRB held constant
Bursty, averaging 50% (campaign C)~50% (15-min avg)1,197 W1,097 W99 W (8.3%)matched-load buckets
24 h call model (campaign C)38-80% per band1,214 W1,157 W57 W (4.7%)ON day carried slightly more data (5,418 vs 5,078 GB)
Per band at idle (ranges over campaigns A, B and the 2026.3.1 re-run):
BandIdle OFFIdle ONSavingBlank symbols (ON)
B1177-182 W104 W73-78 W (about 42%)71-73%
B3181-186 W117-118 W63-67 W (about 36%)71-73%
B8 (10 MHz)118-122 W102-103 W16-18 W (about 14%)65-73%
B28117-120 W104-106 W13-14 W (about 12%)65-73%
B41 TDD164-169 W113 W51-56 W (about 32%)68-72% (DL only)
Load sweep (campaign A): about 228 W at idle, 148 W at 10%, 113 W at 30%, 71 W at 40%, then within noise. At 80% the ON reading was 40 W above OFF, which shows the size of unit noise: a symbol-blanking feature cannot cost power, so negative "savings" are noise.

KPIs: availability, RRC and E-RAB setup, throughput, drops and handover success were equivalent between ON and OFF. Feature control was clean: PA blanking counters were 0 in every OFF window and large in every ON window, and the PA-enable mask read back 0xff (ON) / 0x00 (OFF) before every window.
Level 2 — feature control, blank-symbol maths and analysis rules
Two ways to switch it. Product path: per-cell boolean parameter Microsleep Enable under the cell's additional configuration in ACS/EMS (default false); it needs a reboot, and ACS shows a reboot request. Test path: RU CLI set-usleep-ctrl plus set-usleep-pa-en with a per-radio PA mask (0xff = ON, 0x00 = OFF), no reboot and no service impact observed. Verify every window with get-usleep-ctrl and get-usleep-counters. The campaigns used the CLI to avoid a reboot per toggle; the ACS path was validated separately (USLEEP06 is the operator procedure).

Blank-symbol share = counter increment / (window seconds x 14,000 symbols/s x 4 counters per band). Counters are per radio, so the two bands on one radio report the same value. For TDD B41 the counter has no TDD input and counts UL and guard symbols as blank; remove them: DL-only share = (raw - 38/140) / (102/140) for this frame configuration. Log the time of every counter read: the window length was not recorded and had to be assumed (1,500 s); under load that makes blank shares not comparable.

Design check. Measured idle blank share 65-73% sits inside the 4T4R design estimate of 59-74% (the 2T2R curve, 52-66%, is the wrong reference for this 4T4R unit). The design curve falls roughly linearly to about 7-8% at 60% RB utilisation.

Analysis rules that changed the answers:
• Pair power and PRB over the same 5 minutes. A 5-min power value stamped at the end of its interval belongs with the PRB report period that starts 5 minutes earlier. The run's own report paired them off by one, which misplaced the step edges (an "idle" bin showed 3.4% PRB).
• Compare at the same PRB. ON and OFF never land on exactly the same load (up to 5-9 points apart), and power rises about 1-3 W per PRB point per band (fitted slopes B1 1.7, B3 2.4, B8 2.1, B28 2.4, B41 0.6 W/point). Fit power = a + b x PRB + c x ON over all buckets of a level; the saving is -c with its 95% range. Example: B1 at 50% looked like -6 W raw, but ON ran at 49% vs OFF at 47%; at the same PRB it was -1 ± 6 W, no difference.
• Drop buckets that straddle a toggle, and label ON/OFF from the recorded toggle times or the loop sequence, never from the power level you are trying to measure.
• Check the load actually ran. On 2026.3.1 the B28 "80% OFF" step stayed at about 59% and then went idle, so that row was invalid and had to be excluded from the whole-unit figure.
Level 3 — the B1 MCS side-effect, the low-band puzzle and the third-party baseline
1. B1 runs a lower MCS with uSleep ON. On 2026.3.x, B1 with uSleep ON sent only 5-72% of DL transport blocks at the top of the 256QAM table, against 81-97% with OFF; mean MCS fell by up to 8 indices (22.4 to 14.4 at 20% load) and initial BLER rose 1-2 points. At 20% load B1 carried about 31 Mbps in both states but needed 27% PRB with ON against 18% with OFF. The BLER at each MCS was about the same (9-13%) in both states, so link adaptation is doing its job: the channel the UE reports is worse when uSleep is on. Per-subframe BLER changed shape too: with OFF the errors concentrate on subframes 1 and 6 (~30%); with ON they spread across 2-4 and 7-9 (10-15%). B3 showed a smaller shift at 80% only; B8, B28 and B41 were unaffected. Reproduced on three separate dates. B41 runs a PA wake-up advance of 3000 with zero disable delay and shows no loss, so PA wake timing on B1 is the prime suspect. Lesson: "no KPI impact" on availability and drops is not the same as no impact; look at MCS distribution and PRB cost per Mbps.

2. Low band blanks more but saves less. At idle both radios showed about 73% blank symbols, yet the mid-band radio saved 136 W and the low-band radio 29 W. Raising B28 from 44.7 to 46 dBm did not change the low-band saving (29.5 vs 29 W). A separate B28 test at 15 vs 20 MHz gave 18% vs 16% at idle: bandwidth hardly matters; empty TTIs do. The gap is an open item. One hypothesis (not yet proven) is that the PA bias uSleep can gate is a smaller share of the low-band radio's draw (compare BANDSD01, where uSleep saved 51% on the mid-band radio but 12% on the low-band one).

3. Burstiness creates empty symbols. A steady 50% PRB load saved 0 W because the scheduler spreads data so almost every symbol carries something. Real traffic averaging 50% over 15 minutes saved 99 W, because bursts leave whole TTIs empty between them. Test with realistic traffic, not only flat loads.

4. Third-party single-band RRU baseline. Reference: one single-band third-party 4T4R RRU per band (20 MHz, 46 dBm RS, no PA blanking). Idle draw was about 127 W for B1 and 97 W for B3, rising monotonically to about 400 W at full load. Two such RRUs (B1 + B3) drew 224 W at idle against 360 W for the AAU's B1+B3 radio with uSleep OFF and 221 W with ON. At 30% PRB: AAU ON 438 W, two RRUs 458 W, AAU OFF 497 W. So uSleep is what brings the multi-band AAU to parity at idle. Method: ETSI ES 202 706-1 style static load levels binned at under 5%, 25-35% and 45-55% PRB, average only real 15-min readings, drop toggle-straddling buckets, reject outliers that contradict monotonic power vs load, no curve fit. PM and supply readings can differ by up to 5%. The 50% comparison was inconclusive (one implausible reading).

5. Read results from fits, not single rungs. In a single-band B28 campaign, per-window scatter was 10-27 W, enough to produce spurious negative savings at mid load. Quadratic power-vs-PRB fits per state, or a common-slope model as above, give a far more honest answer than comparing two 15-minute readings.
Interview Q&A
Q: uSleep saves 30% at idle. What would you tell an operator it saves per day?
A: About 57 W per AAU, 4.7%, or about 1.4 kWh per day, measured over a 24 h call model with 38-80% average RB load per band. Idle figures overstate a real day because cells are rarely idle; the saving falls to about 0 at steady 50% load.
Q: Why did a steady 50% load save nothing while bursty traffic averaging 50% saved 99 W?
A: uSleep needs whole empty symbols. A steady load spreads data across nearly every TTI, so the PA is never idle for a full symbol. Bursty traffic leaves complete TTIs empty between bursts, and the PA sleeps in those.
Q: uSleep ON and OFF ran at 49% and 47% PRB, and ON drew 6 W more. Is uSleep costing power?
A: No. Power rises about 1-3 W per PRB point, so a 2-point difference explains it. Fitting both states with a common PRB slope gave -1 ± 6 W, no difference. A blanking feature cannot add power; negative savings are load mismatch or noise.
Q: All standard KPIs pass, yet you suspect a side-effect. Where do you look?
A: At link adaptation: MCS distribution, BLER per MCS and PRB used per Mbps. On B1, uSleep ON moved MCS 3-8 indices lower and needed 27% instead of 18% PRB for the same 31 Mbps, while BLER per MCS stayed the same, meaning the reported channel quality got worse. PA wake timing is the suspect.
Q: How would you count blank symbols on a TDD cell?
A: Read the PA blank counters over a recorded window and divide by window x 14,000 symbols/s x counters. The counter has no TDD input, so UL and guard symbols count as blank; subtract the non-DL share of the frame and divide by the DL share to get the DL-only figure.
ETILT01 E-Tilt (RET/AISG) validation on the 5-band AAU — data path, unit changes, evidence hierarchy and the defects found RCT click to expand ▾
In plain English
Electrical tilt (E-Tilt, also called RET, remote electrical tilt) points the antenna beam slightly down without anyone climbing the mast. Instead of bending the panel, the radio adds a small phase shift across its antenna elements, which steers the beam. Operators manage it through the standard AISG RET workflow: in ACS you see a "RET device" per band and set a tilt in degrees.

Validating it sounds trivial: set 4°, check 4°. In practice the value passes through four pieces of software, changes units twice (degrees, then tenths of a degree), lands in one of two register slots per radio, and is reported back by a management layer that may show the old value. On the 5-band AAU the overall verdict was NOT PASSED: the radio applied tilt correctly, but the readback, naming, persistence and cell-continuity criteria failed or were still open. This card is about how to prove what the radio actually did.
Where the tilt value travels and where it can lie
Drawn from the E-Tilt validation report on the 5-band AAU.
Level 1 — acceptance criteria and the result
Bench: 5-band AAU = three radios (B1+B3, B8+B28, B41). B41 was excluded because of a hardware issue: never judge software behaviour on a unit with a known hardware fault. Test set TLT_001 to TLT_011 under epic GRDEV-9350.
ACCriterionResult
1Midboard register matches the requested tiltPartial: confirmed on B1/B3, B8/B28 pending
2ACS CurTilt reflects the applied tiltFAIL (GRDEV-10271)
3Changing one band does not move the other band on the same radioPASS (B3 at 4° while B1 stayed 0°)
4TX-device writes applied, RX-device writes ignoredPASS (matches firmware design)
5Elevation 0-8° in 1° steps; azimuth unsupportedPending boundary and out-of-range tests
6Cell stays up during a tilt change, no carrier deactivationFAIL (GRDEV-10271)
7Tilt persists over warm reboot, cold power cycle, SW upgradeFAIL (GRDEV-10271)
8AISG inventory: two RET devices per band with correct namesFAIL (GRDEV-10274)
Range. The RU advertises elevation 0° to 8° with 1° granularity (ACS MaxTilt 8.0); azimuth min and max are both 0, i.e. unsupported. An older 0-10° design figure is not the reference for this build; boundary tests cover 0° and 8°, and out-of-range tests check below 0° and above 8°.
Level 2 — mapping, commands and how to verify
AISG device model. The RRH manager emulates four AISG devices per radio and ACS builds its RET inventory from them. The ID format is <RrhSn>-<AldNum>-<Port>-<SubAnt>. Only the TX device applies tilt; the RX device is accepted by the management path but skipped by the firmware. Common inventory values: MinTilt 0.0, MaxTilt 8.0, MechTilt 0.0, SubAnt 4.
RadioSlot 0 (reg 0x0028)Slot 1 (reg 0x002A)TX AISG device / RX device
B1+B3B1B3B1: ...-0-0-4 / ...-1-1-4; B3: ...-2-2-4 / ...-3-3-4
B8+B28B8B28same pattern on that radio's serial
B41B41—...-0-0-4 / ...-1-1-4
Because the bands are spread over three radios, a test must select the RRH serial and the AISG device; the AISG ID alone is not enough. AISG port/ALD number, tilt slot and midboard column are three different mappings: do not mix them up in scripts.

Read and set on the RU (midboard CLI via cli_manager and telnet to local port 8888). Values are whole degrees in, tenths out in hex:
mb-get-aisg-tilt-ant 0 0        # B1 (column 0, slot 0)
mb-get-aisg-tilt-ant 0 1        # B3 (column 0, slot 1)
mb-set-aisg-tilt-ant 2 0 0      # B1 to 2 deg
mb-get-aisg-tilt-ant 0 0        # -> 0x0014  (20 tenths = 2.0 deg)
mb-set-aisg-tilt-ant 4 0 1      # B3 to 4 deg
mb-get-aisg-tilt-ant 0 1        # -> 0x0028  (40 tenths = 4.0 deg)
Two-column check. The test model splits each band's four antennas across two midboard columns (antennas 0-1 and 2-3); ACS shows one RET device per band with SubAnt 4 and the RPC is expected to update both columns. The documentation is inconsistent on whether these AAU variants have one midboard or two, so read the register on column 1 as well and settle it on the bench.

Evidence priority (highest first): (1) midboard register via RU CLI, both columns; (2) NETCONF predefined-beam-tilt-state / elevation-tilt-offset-angle, using capability group 0 or 2 (TX; groups 1 and 3 are RX and skipped); (3) RU beam-manager log, tilt in 0.1° little-endian; (4) ornc AISG_SET_TILT_REQ/RESP, which prove the request, not the result; (5) ACS CurTilt, lowest.

Persistence. The tilt is written to the local database and midboard EEPROM, then pushed to the midboard. At boot it is read back from EEPROM and reported in discovery, so EEPROM is what you check for TLT_005 (warm reboot), TLT_006 (cold cycle) and TLT_007 (SW upgrade). Min/max tilt also live in EEPROM and can only be changed in midboard calibration mode.
Level 3 — defects, false results and log traps
1. ACS shows the old value. After B3 was changed from 6° to 4°, the RU reported 4° and ACS kept showing 6°. ACS CurTilt must not be used as primary evidence until GRDEV-10271 is fixed.

2. False cross-band results. The ACS update routine for RET entries matched the first row by RRH serial only, ignoring port, ALD number and sub-antenna. On a radio with two bands it can overwrite the other band's row, so ACS can show "B1 moved when I tilted B3" when the radio did nothing of the kind. Judge band isolation (TLT_010) from the register, not from ACS.

3. A placeholder band leaks into names. The B28 AISG devices appeared as _B9928_TX / _B9928_RX. The low-band personality file lists band capabilities [8, 9999], and the 9999 placeholder flows into the inventory name. This breaks the naming criterion and any automation that finds devices by band name.

4. Benign I2C errors. The midboard verify-read happens about 1 ms after the write and returned errno 6 on about 38 of 44 writes, yet register and NETCONF readbacks confirmed the tilt. Track it (GRDEV-10353), but do not fail a tilt on that log line alone.

5. Log capture. ornc logs rotate quickly; grab evidence straight after each step. Entries appear in both bare tai64n and syslog-prefixed form, so grep with grep -rah without anchoring to the start of the line. A tai64n token is @ followed by 16 hex digits of seconds and 8 of nanoseconds; Unix seconds = first 16 hex digits minus 0x4000000000000000.
Interview Q&A
Q: ACS says the tilt is 6° and the RU says 4°. Which do you believe and how do you prove it?
A: The RU. Read the midboard register for that band's slot on both columns (0x0028 = 40 tenths = 4.0°) and cross-check the NETCONF elevation-tilt-offset-angle in a TX capability group. ACS CurTilt was shown to keep stale values, and the ornc response says success without confirming the radio applied it.
Q: Why can a 2° request appear as 20 in one log and 0x0014 in another?
A: The ornc request carries tenths of a degree, so 2° is 20; the midboard register stores tenths in hex, so 20 is 0x0014. ACS and the ornc response use whole degrees. Always note the unit at each layer.
Q: How would you test per-band isolation on a two-band radio?
A: Set one band (e.g. B3 to 4°) and read both slots from the register: B3 slot 1 should change and B1 slot 0 should not. Do not use ACS for this, because its row-update bug can overwrite the other band's entry and fake a cross-band change.
Q: Which store must you check for tilt persistence after reboot and upgrade?
A: The midboard EEPROM. Tilt is written there and reloaded into the database at boot, then reported in discovery. Check it after warm reboot, cold power cycle and software upgrade.
Q: Why was B41 excluded and why does that matter?
A: It had a hardware issue. A hardware fault can make correct software look broken (or hide a software bug), so its results cannot be used to grade the feature. Exclude it explicitly and say so in the report.
AAUTS01 AAU Productisation Test Strategy — five pillars (RCT, E2E, scale, stability, customer band plan) and what a manufacturing test set can and cannot prove for TS 36.141 RCT click to expand ▾
In plain English
Before a new radio is shipped to a customer, someone has to decide what to test, with which equipment, and what counts as done. This card is a worked example: the test strategy for productising a 4-band AAU (B1, B3, B8, B41) for a customer, organised as five pillars — RF conformance, end-to-end functions, scale/mobility, stability and the customer's band plan.

Its most useful lesson is about the instrument. The lab RF tester was an EXM-class one-box wireless test set (see EXM). It is a manufacturing test set, not a conformance test system: its measurement uncertainty does not meet TS 36.141 Table 4.1.2-1, so every RF number it produces is engineering data, not conformance evidence. The strategy therefore lists, clause by clause, what the box can prove, what needs an extra licence, and what needs extra hardware — and it shows that one extra signal generator unblocks five clauses. For the full RCT campaign on an AAU see FCAAU01; for a quick go/no-go see SMOKE01.
Figure — five pillars on a shared lab foundation
Each pillar has its own objective, method and exit criteria; RCT is limited by the instrument (see Level 3).
Level 1 — the device and the five pillars
What is inside the AAU (it decides what you can test): eCPRI O-RAN fronthaul into an RFSoC (Linux + FPGA) that runs CFR, DPD and the NETCONF/YANG M-plane; a mid-board MCU supervising PA bias, temperature sensors and RFFE GPIO over RS485 to four RFFE modules (GaN PA + DAC/ADC monitor + phase shifters). So "RF" faults can come from DPD on the RFSoC, bias from the MCU, or the RFFE itself.
PillarObjectiveTypical contentExit criterion
RCT (automated)TS 36.141 mandatory clausesch 6 TX: power, EVM, ACLR, SEM, spurious, TAE; ch 7 RX: REFSENS, dynamic range, ACS, blocking, RX spurious; ch 8 PUSCH/PRACH/PUCCH under fadingpass with margin on what the instrument can measure; gaps listed explicitly
E2Ethe RU behaves correctly as a productNETCONF HW config and persistence, FH disconnect / SFP hot-pull / flap, under/over-voltage and power cut with dying-gasp alarm, SW download/install/activate/rollback, FM alarm raise/clear for every phase-1 alarm, sync FREERUN→LOCKED→HOLDOVER→FREERUN with TX gating, invalid NETCONF rejection, watchdog reboot, call-home retryevery alarm raised and cleared, every recovery returns to service unaided
Scale / mobility3-sector behaviour with real UEssingle/multi-UE attach per band at 5/10/15/20 MHz; CA B1+B3 2CC at each BW; intra/inter-freq X2 and S1 HO, CSFB to the 2G band, inter-RAT, VoLTE during HO, B41 TDD HO; 32-UE iPerf call models (400/100/50/25 s, flight-mode and inactivity-timer variants)success rates and throughput per scenario
Stabilitynothing degrades over time24 h soaks per band/CA, VoLTE 12 h, 3-sector 48 h; CPU, memory and log growth sampled every 15 minzero unexpected alarms; NETCONF read-back after soak identical to before (zero drift)
Customer configthe exact band plan orderedB1+B3+B8+B41 full bring-up; B8 2G voice and GPRS/EDGE; CSFB LTE→B8 and re-attach; 2G/4G co-existence on one RUcustomer scenarios pass end to end
Power vs load is measured at PRB load 0 %, 50 %, 100 % and as a sweep — it shows PA bias and DPD behaviour and feeds the energy figures.
Level 2 — clause-by-clause: what a one-box manufacturing tester can do for TS 36.141
Build this matrix before promising an RCT scope. Values are from the B1 engineering runs (FDD); limits are the TS 36.141 / 36.104 figures.
ClauseTestOne-box testerWhy / result
6.2Output power (FDD bands)YESfunctional verification
6.5Frequency errorYESworst 42 Hz against the 228 Hz limit used in the plan — comfortable
6.6EVMYESworst 2.06 % against the clause limit used in the plan (2.75 %) — watch this margin; it moves with DPD/CFR tuning, temperature and PA bias
6.7DL RS powerYESall configurations passed
6.8Occupied bandwidthYESquick win — not yet run
6.9ACLRYES55–57 dBc against 45 dBc — good margin
6.10Operating band unwanted emissions (SEM)LICENCEneeds the SEM measurement licence on the analyser — check before planning
6.11Transmitter spurious emissionsNOharmonics need an analyser above the 6 GHz hardware limit
6.12Transmitter intermodulationNOneeds a second signal generator as the interferer
6.13Time alignment error (TAE)PARTIALdata captured, formal pass/fail report pending
7.2Reference sensitivityYESB1 and B3 pass
7.3Receiver dynamic rangePARTIALonly one channel done; bottom/top channels pending
7.4, 7.5, 7.6, 7.8In-channel selectivity, ACS/narrow-band blocking, blocking, RX intermodulationNOall need a modulated/CW interferer from a second generator
7.7Receiver spurious emissionsYESno interferer needed — quick win, not yet run
ch 8PUSCH / PUCCH / PRACH performanceNOneeds a fading channel emulator
B41 (TDD), NRany TDD or NR measurementLICENCELTE-TDD and NR measurement applications not licensed — hardware tunes, software cannot measure
Procurement arithmetic: a second signal generator unblocks five clauses at once (6.12, 7.4, 7.5, 7.6, 7.8); an analyser above 6 GHz unblocks 6.11; a fading emulator unblocks all of chapter 8; two software licences unblock SEM and B41. That list is the deliverable a test lead takes to management. (Note: the source grouped 7.4–7.8 together, but 7.7 RX spurious needs no interferer and can run today.)

Other E2E checks worth copying: FM alarm lifecycle for each phase-1 fault id (in this program ids 1, 2, 4, 11, 12, 17, 18, 2001–2005 and 29 — see CM20 for meanings); config persistence by diffing a full NETCONF read-back before and after a soak; a 15-minute resource sampler (CPU, memory, log size) during every soak.
Level 3 — the judgement calls behind the plan
  • Manufacturing vs conformance instruments. TS 36.141 §4.1.2 sets a maximum test-system uncertainty per clause (Table 4.1.2-1) and a test-tolerance rule for applying it. A production tester is optimised for speed and repeatability on a known-good design, not for that uncertainty budget, and the vendor itself advised against using it for formal RCT. Consequence: label all results "engineering data", and budget a conformance lab or a conformance-grade analyser/generator set for the formal report.
  • Margin, not pass/fail, is the useful number. 42 Hz vs 228 Hz and 55 dBc vs 45 dBc are safe; 2.06 % vs 2.75 % EVM is not, because it will move with DPD state, temperature and unit-to-unit spread. Put such clauses on a per-unit watch list (compare SMOKE01).
  • Choose B/M/T channels per direction. Receiver clauses must run on uplink channels; the plan quoted downlink-band frequencies for 7.3, which is a frequent copy-paste slip. Check every RX channel against the band's UL range before running.
  • TDD and multi-RAT need their own software. B41 could be tuned but not measured; 2G on B8 needs a GSM application too. Inventory the licences per band and RAT at the start, not when the campaign reaches that band.
  • Stability exit criteria must be binary. "Zero unexpected alarms" and "zero NETCONF drift after soak" are unambiguous; "stable" is not.
  • Automation reuse. RF clauses are driven by Python/SCPI (see AUTO05, EXM); mobility by scripted HO loops and iPerf call models across 32 UEs in a chamber with a programmable attenuator (see AUTO11 for attenuator-driven coverage).
Interview Q&A
Q: Can you sign off TS 36.141 conformance with a one-box manufacturing tester?
A: No. Its test-system uncertainty does not meet TS 36.141 Table 4.1.2-1, so results are engineering data only. Use it for functional verification and margin tracking, and do the formal campaign on conformance-grade equipment.
Q: Which 36.141 clauses need a second signal generator and why?
A: TX intermodulation 6.12 and the receiver interference tests 7.4 in-channel selectivity, 7.5 ACS/narrow-band blocking, 7.6 blocking and 7.8 RX intermodulation — they all need a wanted signal plus an interferer. One generator purchase unblocks all five.
Q: EVM measured 2.06 % against a 2.75 % limit. Pass — anything else to do?
A: It passes but with thin margin. Track it per unit and over temperature and DPD state, and re-check after any CFR/DPD or PA-bias change.
Q: Name the five pillars of an AAU productisation test strategy.
A: RF conformance (RCT), end-to-end product functions (NETCONF config, FH recovery, power events, SW lifecycle, alarms, sync, watchdog), scale/mobility (CA, handovers, VoLTE, multi-UE call models), stability (24/48 h soaks with zero drift and zero unexpected alarms) and the customer's band-plan configuration.
Q: How do you prove configuration persistence after a soak?
A: Take a full NETCONF read-back of the running configuration before the soak and again after; diff them. Any difference is a failure (zero drift permitted).
ULIQCAP01 Uplink IQ capture from the 5G PHY — rx_grid / PRACH / PUCCH / PUSCH dumps turned into replayable test vectors (capture_rxgrid.py, ctrlApp, cap_read) RCT click to expand ▾
In plain English
When a 5G cell fails to decode uplink in the field or on the bench (PUCCH format 2 errors, PUSCH CRC failures, missed PRACH), the logs only tell you that it failed. The uplink IQ collection tool lets you ask the running 5G PHY to dump exactly what it received: the frequency-domain RX resource grid (IQ per subcarrier per symbol), the PRACH grid, and the PUSCH / PUCCH / PRACH configurations the MAC asked it to decode in those slots. A converter then turns the dumps into per-slot test vectors (sfnX_slotY_IQdataF.bin + sfnX_slotY_ul_tti.json) which you can replay into the PHY in dummy mode, or feed into a MATLAB uplink simulator. In short: it turns a one-off live failure into a reproducible offline test case.

Think of it as a "black-box flight recorder" for the uplink receiver: you capture the air interface as the PHY saw it, plus the instructions it was given, and then re-fly the same slot as many times as you like while you change the receiver code.
Capture chain: from a live cell to a replayable test vector
All tools ship inside the PHY package (bin/nr5g/gnb/tools) and are copied to /var/log/tools when l1.sh starts, so they are reachable from the host.
Level 1 — core facts
What the PHY can dump (default capture points):
Capture pointWhat it holdsWhy you want it
rx_gridFrequency-domain IQ of the whole UL slot after FFT, per antennaThe raw evidence: replay it and you re-run the exact receiver input
rx_prach_gridPRACH occasion IQ gridReproduce missed / false PRACH detections (see PRACHDM01)
pusch_configThe PUSCH PDUs the MAC requested for that slot (RNTI, PRBs, MCS, DMRS ...)Without it you have IQ but do not know what to decode
pucch_configPUCCH PDUs (format, PRBs, symbols, UCI sizes)Needed to replay HARQ-ACK / CSI decoding
prach_configPRACH configuration for the occasionDetector parameters for replay
What you get on the host: a captures_phynodeXX/ folder per PHY node containing a timestamped .tgz. Inside: the raw capture_dump_<point>_NNNN.bin files (one rx_grid file per captured slot index) and an in/ folder of decoded, replayable pairs sfnX_slotY_IQdataF.bin + sfnX_slotY_ul_tti.json.
The ul_tti JSON follows the SCF FAPI UL_TTI.request shape the PHY already understands, so the replayed slot looks to the PHY exactly like a live slot from the MAC. If a slot carried several PUSCH/PUCCH/PRACH PDUs, the converter builds a multi-PDU message.
Control path: capture is switched on and off through ctrlApp talking to the PHY control port (default 12345); the capture window is a few seconds, so you get a burst of consecutive slots, not a continuous recording.
Level 2 — how to capture, decode and replay
1. Quick capture from the setup tool (Kubernetes rig). Run on the DU host; one capture per PHY node listed:
nr_setup_tools.py -R 02          # capture on phynode02
nr_setup_tools.py -R 02 03       # phynode02 and phynode03 in one go
# older rigs may still have the k8s variant of the setup tool; same -R idea

ls captures_phynode02/
  <timestamp>.tgz                 # unpack: capture_dump_*.bin + in/
2. Drive capture_rxgrid.py directly when you need more control (it lives under the pod shared directory, e.g. .../pods/phy/phynode02/tools/):
OptionMeaningWhen to use
-n <nodes>PHY nodes to capture (02, 03, 04; default 02)Multi-cell DU
-bDecode the binaries right after captureDefault from the setup tool; memory heavy, host only
-d <dir>Decode an existing (unpacked) capture directoryCapture fast now, decode offline later
-c "a b c"Replace the default capture list with your ownGrab internal receiver stages (below)
-l <logdir>Local mode: give the directory the PHY writes captures toRCT / non-K8s PHY run with l1.sh -rct
-p <port>ctrlApp port if not 12345Only if someone changed the PHY control port
-mLeave messy: keep files that do not line up with rx_gridDebugging the alignment itself
3. Capture internal receiver stages. Beyond the default five points, the PHY exposes intermediate buffers. Example for a PUCCH format 2 investigation:
capture_rxgrid.py -c "rx_grid pusch_config pucch_config pucch_f2_ls_est pucch_f2_ifft_out \n                     pucch_f2_chan_est pucch_f2_pdp pucch_f2_equ_out"
# no -b here: binary capture only, then later:
capture_rxgrid.py -d ./unpacked_capture_dir
The F2 chain points map to the receiver steps: least-squares DMRS estimate, IFFT to the delay domain, channel estimate, power-delay profile, equaliser output. Comparing them with a MATLAB reference tells you which stage diverges.
4. Replay. Point the PHY in dummy (test-MAC) mode, or the MATLAB UL simulator, at the in/ folder. Same slot in, deterministic result out; change one receiver parameter at a time and compare CRC / UCI results.
Level 3 — pitfalls, alignment and a real use
  • Do not decode inside the pod. cap_read output (JSON) is large; the tool deliberately redirects it to the host. Running -b inside the PHY pod can fill the pod filesystem and take the cell down with it.
  • SFN/slot misalignment. Because each capture point has its own buffer and timing, config captures and rx_grid captures do not always cover exactly the same SFN/slot. The script trims any file not aligned with rx_grid; if a slot you expected is missing, re-run with -m and check the SFN/slot stamps yourself before blaming the decoder.
  • Short window. Capture lasts a few seconds. For a rare failure, trigger the capture repeatedly while the failure KPI is rising, or reproduce the condition (attenuation, interference) so it happens in every slot.
  • Load matters. Capturing costs PHY real-time budget; avoid capturing during a latency-critical throughput measurement and expect the run to be slightly perturbed.
  • Ownership of the tools. They are copied to /var/log/tools by l1.sh, so they always match the running PHY build — use that copy, not one from an older package.

Where it fits in RU / RCT validation. RCT measures UL sensitivity and PRACH detection against a signal generator (see RCT02, PHYT01, PRACHDM01). When a sensitivity point fails and the RF path checks out, an IQ capture separates "the RU delivered bad IQ" (spurs, wrong gain, saturation visible in rx_grid) from "the PHY decoded good IQ badly" (rx_grid clean, later stage diverges). The same family of debug tools also extracts SRS channel estimates (CIR/CFR) from the L1 debug data on massive-MIMO setups, and an L1-L2 FAPI capture (see FHCAP01) can likewise be turned into test vectors.

Illustrative case (how you would use it): live cell shows HARQ-ACK on PUCCH F2 failing at moderate SINR. Capture with the F2 points, replay offline: rx_grid power and DMRS look correct, but the power-delay profile shows the timing peak wrapped to the end of the window — a timing-offset estimate issue, fixed in the receiver, and the captured slot becomes a permanent regression vector.
Interview Q&A
Q: Why capture both rx_grid and pusch_config / pucch_config?
A: The IQ alone is not decodable without knowing what was scheduled (RNTI, PRBs, MCS, DMRS, UCI sizes). The configs become the ul_tti JSON that tells the replayed PHY what to decode in each slot.
Q: Why must decode (-b) not run inside the PHY pod?
A: The decoded JSON is large and memory heavy; inside the pod it can exhaust memory/disk and disturb the real-time PHY. The tool writes decoded output on the host instead.
Q: A captured slot shows a clean rx_grid but the decode fails on replay. What next?
A: The RU/IQ path is fine; capture intermediate stages (channel estimate, PDP, equaliser output) with -c and compare to a reference model to find the receiver stage that diverges.
Q: Some config files were deleted after capture. Why?
A: Capture buffers are not perfectly SFN/slot aligned; files that do not line up with the rx_grid timestamps are removed. Use -m to keep them when investigating alignment.
Q: How does this help UL sensitivity testing?
A: It splits a failed sensitivity point into RF/IQ problems (visible in the raw grid) versus decoder problems (clean grid, bad decode), and gives a replayable vector for regression.
